📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Marburger Farm and Ethan Good Photography.

Texas-based antique and design show Marburger Farm has unveiled an exhibition building made partly from salvaged materials sourced directly from across the 43-acre property, as shown in this video produced by Dezeen.

Called Gage Hall, the building’s facade is made from reclaimed timber sourced from around the farm and is topped with a traditional Texas metal roof and contemporary skylight elements that bring natural light into the hall.

Industry observers note that the hall brings an additional 7,500 square feet of shopping space to Marburger Farm, bringing the fair’s total space to 100,000 square feet. Designed to honour the site’s dairy farm heritage, the hall also showcases its vision for the future.

The antique and design show has become a destination for international designers looking to source unique interior objects including furniture, lighting and vintage textiles.

The 43-acre show is located in Round Top, Texas, and has attracted designers such as Kelly Wearstler and Leanne Ford.

The fair offers visitors access to objects from over 200 independent dealers and has become one of the largest antique reveals in the United States.

The site also includes a Texas-style town square, 10 restored historic buildings, four tents and a 150-year-old saloon, which has been restored to its original use as a social space and bar.

Founded in 1997, the show has grown to attract over 30,000 people annually.

The antique show takes place in January, March and October each year.

Marburger Farm is owned by Brook Partners, a Dallas-based investment firm focusing on culture and commerce.

The company also runs the upcoming Dallas Art Fair, which is held from 15 to 18 April 2027 in Dallas, Texas. To learn more, visit the Marburger Farm website.

Marburger Farm Antique Show took place from 27 to 31 October in Round Top, Texas. The winter show will take place 21-24 January and the spring show will take place 23-27 March 2027. See Dezeen Events Guide for an up-to-date list of architecture and design events taking place around the world.

This video was produced by Dezeen as part of a partnership with Marburger Farm. Find out more about Dezeen partnership content here.

Photography by Marburger Farm and Ethan Good Photography.

Why Accessibility Is An Operational Capability, Not A Feature

📅 2026-06-30 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2204 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that mikhail Prosmitskiy is a Software Engineer who loves making complex things feel simple — and fast.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • This article has been kindly supported by our dear friends at Level Access, who help organizations create accessible and legally compliant websites, mobile apps, software, and other digital experiences.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that mikhail Prosmitskiy is a Software Engineer who loves making complex things feel simple — and fast. He’s spent years building everything from crypto … More about Mikhail ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

This article has been kindly supported by our dear friends at Level Access, who help organizations create accessible and legally compliant websites, mobile apps, software, and other digital experiences. Thank you!

We know that right now, a senior engineer is shipping a checkout flow they “built” in a single afternoon. AI assistant does the heavy lifting, happy path runs clean, and a rotating chevron spins on the order summary. Two weeks later, engineering gets a notice from customer support: a blind customer using a screen reader can’t complete the purchase because the “Pay Now” control is a with a click handler. No role. Not focusable. Not working.

That gap — between code that runs and a product people can actually use — is becoming one of the defining engineering challenges of the AI era. Teams can generate UI faster than ever, but they still have to guarantee that what they ship is usable, secure, and maintainable.

Accessibility sits right in the middle of that problem.

This is not an article about compliance checklists or end-of-project audits. It’s about engineering systems. Specifically, why accessibility should be treated as an operational capability — alongside privacy, security, reliability, and observability — and what that looks like in practice.

Industry observers note that for years, the default way to “do” accessibility was the one-time, audit-only approach: hire a firm, get a list of 200 findings, fix some of them, file the report. A lot of teams have now moved beyond this model — and the reason is worth looking into.

Recent findings suggest that audits do matter. For sales, procurement, governance — they’re essential. When a buyer asks for a VPAT or an ACR, you need one. When legal asks if you’re meeting requirements, you need documentation. Audits serve those purposes well.

But audits don’t help you build accessible features during sprint planning. Audits can cost points during a sprint. They don’t catch problems before merge requests. They don’t scale with deployment velocity. The mistake, essentially, is tackling accessibility as a snapshot when you really need constant monitoring. Six months after the audit, the product has shipped dozens of releases, multiple new features, and a redesigned nav. The report is now fiction. Compliance is not a state you reach — it’s a state you maintain, and complexity fights you the whole way.

Recent findings suggest that the WebAIM Million report, which scans the top one million home pages every year, found that 95.9% of pages had detectable WCAG failures in its 2026 run, with an average of 56.1 errors per page. The number of page elements jumped more than 20% in a single year, likely driven by AI-enabled development and ‘vibe coding’ — and more elements mean more places to break. Accessibility debt behaves exactly like technical debt: every inaccessible component you ship becomes a future remediation project, and the interest compounds.

Any strategy that treats accessibility as a periodic event rather than a continuous property of the system is going to lose.

With the scale at which teams now generate UI, the gap doesn’t just persist; it multiplies.

Recent findings suggest that start with how fast this arrived. In February 2025, Andrej Karpathy coined “vibe coding” — a way of working where you “fully give in to the vibes” and “forget that the code even exists”. You describe intent, the model generates, you accept the diffs without reading them. It was meant for weekend projects. It did not stay there. Y Combinator reported that 25% of its Winter 2025 batch had codebases that were 95% AI-generated.

Models don’t land on non-semantic markup by accident — three forces push them there. Most React code on GitHub uses non-semantic “soup”, so that’s what the models learn. Human reviewers and evaluators judge output visually, so the feedback loop rewards looks, not semantics. And is fewer tokens than , so absent a constraint, the model takes the cheap path.

Here’s the thing about AI-generated UI: it’s inaccessible by default. Not occasionally — by default. A developer writing in Frontend Masters tested AI-generated React components across multiple tools and documented the pattern. A typical AI-generated sidebar had ten distinct accessibility failures in twenty-nine lines: no landmark, no heading, no list structure, elements with click handlers instead of buttons, no aria-expanded, no keyboard handling, and unlabeled icons. The accessibility tree — the structure screen readers actually read — came back as flat, unstructured text. “Same pixels” as the author put it. “One is a door. The other is a painting of a door”.

Now connect this to security, because the two failures come from the same root. Veracode’s 2025 GenAI Code Security Report tested large language models across dozens of coding tasks and found that a large fraction of AI-generated code introduced security vulnerabilities — including OWASP Top 10 flaws. Cross-site scripting failures were particularly common, and security performance did not meaningfully improve with newer, larger models. The glitch wasn’t model intelligence. It was process: developers generating code without specifying security constraints and accepting output without systematic verification.

The same shortcut that skips the security review skips the accessibility review. At scale, AI won’t close the accessibility gap — it has industrialized the very thing that creates it.

According to recent reports, the fix is not to ban AI. Your developers are already using it. The fix is to constrain it and verify it — to treat AI as a very fast teammate who always needs guardrails.

This is usually where someone claims, “Guardrails? Sounds great, but they will slow us down.”.

In practice, the opposite tends to be true.

Shift-left is the entire DevOps thesis, and it applies cleanly here. An accessibility matter caught during design review is a comment. The same issue found in production is a remediation project.

Recent findings suggest that catching an accessibility concern as a component is built takes minutes. Fixing one after the fact — discovering it in an audit, diagnosing the root cause, restructuring the markup, applying the necessary fix, writing tests — can easily take hours. Multiply that across hundreds of findings from a late-stage audit, and you have weeks of unplanned work that earlier automated checks — whether in design reviews, development workflows, or CI — could have prevented.

It has been revealed that teams that integrate accessibility into everyday workflows avoid the expensive surprises: emergency audits, remediation sprints, procurement blockers, and redesigns that quietly break core user journeys. Accessibility doesn’t reduce velocity. Unexpected work reduces velocity. In-flow accessibility is one way of eliminating unexpected work.

The organizations that scale accessibility successfully do not rely on heroes. They rely on systems.

Sources indicate that the highest-leverage place to start is the design system. One accessible component can be reused thousands of times. The GOV.UK Design System is a useful example: components undergo both automated and manual testing using assistive technologies such as JAWS, NVDA, VoiceOver, and TalkBack. The team is explicit about the limits of automation and supplements tooling with user testing involving people with disabilities. They’re equally clear that using the design system doesn’t “magically” make a service accessible; it just gives you a higher starting point.

Sources indicate that accessibility becomes infrastructure. That’s the lesson.

From there, it moves into the engineering workflow:.

Finally, accessibility becomes enforceable through automation:.

At that point, accessibility stops depending on memory and starts depending on the process. It becomes part of your platform.

A few implementation patterns consistently show up in teams that do this well.

Industry observers note that instead of fixing accessibility after generation, bake requirements directly into tooling through Cursor rules, Copilot instructions, or repository-level standards. Tell the model to use semantic HTML. Tell it when to use buttons versus links. Tell it to expose the state and labels correctly. Models follow persistent constraints far more reliably than one-off prompts.

Sources indicate that comboboxes, menus, tabs, modals, and similar controls routinely become accessibility hotspots. Libraries such as Radix UI, React Aria, and Headless UI already solve many of these problems. The scalable approach is not about repeatedly implementing accessibility correctly. It’s inheriting accessible behavior from well-tested primitives.

Sources indicate that focus order, labels, heading hierarchy, and interaction states should be specified before implementation begins. If accessibility requirements are absent from the design artifact, they are often absent from the final product. A simple memo at design handoff — what is the tab order, what are the labels, what happens on error — removes a huge amount of guesswork later.

Recent findings suggest that none of these patterns is exotic. They’re just DevOps and platform thinking applied to accessibility.

Recent findings suggest that engineering leaders rarely prioritize accessibility solely because of regulations. But regulations, procurement requirements, user retention, and product quality all point in the same direction.

In a recent development, legal pressure continues to increase. Digital accessibility lawsuits in the United States have stayed in the thousands per year, and they are not limited to large enterprises. The European Accessibility Act is now enforceable across the EU, applying to e‑commerce, banking, ticketing, telecoms, and more, regardless of where the company is headquartered. The message is clear: accessibility is no longer a “nice-to-have” in the eyes of regulators.

But compliance is only part of the story. The bigger story is the market you leave on the table. The World Economic Forum (December 2023) estimates that the world’s 1.3 billion people with disabilities, “along with their friends and family, has a spending power of $13 trillion”; disabled consumers alone control roughly $8 trillion in annual disposable income, per the Valuable 500.

Industry observers note that in the UK alone, the Click-Away Pound Report 2019 found the “Click-Away Pound has risen to £17.1 billion” — more than 4.9 million people with access needs who abandon inaccessible sites and spend elsewhere, up almost 45% from £11.75 billion in 2016. People don’t file a bug report. They leave and buy from a competitor.

Sources indicate that there is also a procurement reality that turns accessibility from a cost into a moat. If you sell B2B or to government, you will increasingly be asked for proof of accessibility — VPATs/ACRs or equivalent documentation. According to Level Access’s Seventh Annual State of Digital Accessibility Report, 75% of organizations now require proof of accessibility at least most of the time when purchasing digital products — essentially unchanged from 74% in the previous report, but with a notable shift towards stricter enforcement, as those that always require it rose from 27% to 31%. A strong ACR accelerates the sales cycle; a weak one, or none at all, creates redlines that stall or kill it. For some buyers, this is a hard requirement before your product can even enter evaluation. A strong accessibility story accelerates the sales cycle. A weak one creates redlines that stall or kill it.

Step back and the deeper pattern is clear: accessibility is a proxy for engineering maturity. A team that ships semantic HTML, manages focus, exposes state correctly, and tests it in CI is a team that has its house in order. The same discipline that produces an accessible component produces a maintainable, testable, less buggy one.

Sources indicate that for dev and product leaders, that’s the real business case: accessibility work is platform work. It pays off every time a feature ships faster and more smoothly, with less rework, than it otherwise would have.

Recent findings suggest that if you take one thing from this, make it this: accessibility doesn’t come from an audit, a hero, or a heroic remediation sprint before launch. It comes from systems.

Recent findings suggest that an accessible design system so components start right. A Definition of Done so they stay right. Automated testing and CI gates so regressions fail the build. Governance, so someone owns it. Guardrails for AI-assisted development so your fastest tool stops being your biggest liability.

Industry observers note that none of those practices is particularly glamorous. That’s exactly why they work. They’re the same kinds of boring, reliable systems you already trust for security, reliability, and performance.

But there’s one thing no tool on that list can do. No linter, no automated scanner run, no dashboard will ever tell you what it’s actually like to use your product as a blind person with a screen reader, or to navigate your checkout with a keyboard because a tremor makes a mouse inoperable. So build the systems — you need them, and they’re the only way accessibility survives contact with a real release schedule. But test with real people with disabilities regularly. The first time you sit behind someone using JAWS to fight through a form your team thought was “done”, something changes. The tooling tells you whether you passed. A real person tells you whether it actually works.

Accessibility is not a feature. It’s an operational capability. Treat it that way, and you get something dev and product leaders already care about: a faster, safer, more reliable way to ship software.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A painting by the German Impressionist painter Max Slevogt, which has been restituted to the heirs of Eduard Fuchs—a collector, Communist and writer who fled Nazi Germany with his Jewish wife—will be auctioned next month. Slevogt's Paradiesvögel (Birds of Paradise, 1900), was acquired by the Von der Heydt-Museum in Wuppertal, western Germany, in 2006 and following an investigation that began in 2020 was approved for restitution by the Wuppertal city council on 13 July 2026. Paradiesvögel will be offered at Ketterer Kunst's 5 December Day Sale with an estimate of €40,000–€60,000.

Recent findings suggest that given the large number of heirs a sale was the only option, Ketterer Kunst's head of communications Anja Häse tells The Art Newspaper. The heirs consigned the painting once the restitution was completed, she adds. Another work by Slevogt from Fuchs’s collection, Don Quichotte und die Schafherde (Don Quixote and the Flock of Sheep, 1907) is also included in the auction with an estimate of €20,000–€30,000. According to Ketterer Kunst's provenance information, a settlement was reached between the current private owners and Fuchs's heirs in 2026, allowing the work to be offered at auction free of restitution claims. The terms of the “amicable restitution” have not been disclosed.

Max Slevogt's Don Quichotte und die Schafherde (Don Quixote and the Flock of Sheep, 1907) © Ketterer Kunst.

In a recent development, fuchs's collection was confiscated by the Nazis but later released. In 1937, he was forced to sell works from the collection to pay a punitive emigration tax imposed by the Nazi authorities. Paradiesvögel was auctioned in Berlin in June 1937 and acquired by the art dealer Hildebrand Gurlitt, passing to Fritz Slevogt in 1939.

Paradiesvögel was included in a sale at Kunsthaus Lempertz in December 2004, estimated at €100,000-€120,000, but went unsold. According to Meyer, the work remained in the auction house’s custody afterwards and was subsequently exhibited at the Von der Heydt-Museum in 2005. The museum then purchased the painting through the auction house in 2006 for €120,000. Meyer says that while the painting's provenance was documented in the 2004 auction catalogue, the museum can no longer establish whether a provenance check was carried out before the acquisition or how thoroughly it was assessed. She also confirmed that the museum is not considering any legal action against Kunsthaus Lempertz regarding due diligence on the painting.

The provenance investigation began after Fuchs's heirs contacted the institution in 2020, the museum's press officer Marion Meyer tells The Art Newspaper. The research drew on a wider project, supported by the German Lost Art Foundation, to reconstruct Eduard and Margarete Fuchs's collection.

Recent findings suggest that “Restituting Max Slevogt's Paradiesvögel means losing a painting, but we gain something far more important: the certainty that we have acted responsibly towards history,” the Von der Heydt-Museum's director Roland Mönig indicates in a press statement. He describes provenance research as “an essential part of our work”.

Industry observers note that in 2024, the Staatsgalerie Stuttgart restituted Slevogt's Der verlorene Sohn (The Prodigal Son, 1899) to Fuchs's heirs. The triptych was sold at Ketterer Kunst later that year.

"Is Social Security taxable?" is one of the most common tax questions retirees ask — and the answer frustrates almost everyone: it depends. Depending on your total income, anywhere from 0% to 85% of your Social Security benefits can be subject to federal income tax. The tax was introduced in 1983, originally affecting about 10% of recipients. Today, because the income thresholds were never indexed for inflation, roughly 56% of Social Security recipients pay tax on their benefits.

Sources indicate that the good news: even in the worst case, you'll never pay tax on 100% of your Social Security. The bad news: the formula for calculating the taxable amount is one of the most convoluted in the entire tax code. In this guide, we'll break it down into plain English, show you exactly how to calculate what you owe, and — most importantly — share strategies the FI community uses to reduce or eliminate the tax entirely.

Industry observers note that the IRS uses a special formula called "combined income" (also called "provisional income") to determine how much of your Social Security benefits are taxable. Here's the formula:.

Combined Income = Adjusted Gross Income (AGI) + Nontaxable Interest + Half of Social Security Benefits.

The resulting number determines which taxation tier you fall into. Notice that the thresholds haven't changed since 1993 — they are not adjusted for inflation, which means more retirees cross into taxable territory every year.

Important: "Up to 85% taxed" does not mean you pay an 85% tax rate. It means 85% of your benefits are added to your taxable income and taxed at your ordinary income rate. If you're in the 22% bracket and 85% of your $30,000 benefit is taxable, you'd owe 22% on $25,500 — roughly $5,610.

Industry observers note that this is the most common Social Security tax confusion. When the IRS states "up to 85% of benefits are taxable," it means 85% of your benefit amount gets added to your taxable income and taxed at your regular rate. If your marginal rate is 22% and 85% of your $30,000 benefit is taxable, you owe about $5,610 — not $25,500. The effective tax rate on your full benefit in this example is about 18.7%.

Industry observers note that let's walk through a real example. Meet Sarah: she's 67, single, retired, and receives $24,000 per year in Social Security benefits. She also has $18,000 in IRA withdrawals and $2,000 in municipal bond interest.

In a recent development, sarah adds $3,500 to her other taxable income. At a 12% marginal rate, that's roughly $420 in additional federal tax on her Social Security.

Beyond federal taxes, 13 states also tax Social Security benefits to some degree as of 2026. Each state has its own thresholds and exemption amounts:.

The remaining 37 states and Washington, D.C. do not tax Social Security benefits at all. If you're planning where to retire, this is a meaningful factor — especially if you have substantial SS benefits combined with other retirement income.

Industry observers note that the FI community has identified several strategies that can significantly reduce the tax bite on Social Security benefits. The key insight: since taxation is based on combined income, controlling your income in retirement is the lever.

This is the single most powerful strategy. Roth IRA withdrawals are not included in the combined income formula. If you retire early (before Social Security age), you have a window of low-income years to convert Traditional IRA/401(k) money to Roth.

Recent findings suggest that example: Between ages 55 and 67, you convert $500,000 from your Traditional IRA to a Roth — paying tax at rates as low as 10-12%. When you claim Social Security at 67, your Roth withdrawals don't push you into a higher SS taxation tier. Instead of 85% of your benefits being taxable, you might pay tax on 0-50%.

The math is dramatic over a 25+ year retirement. Converting at 12% during early retirement to avoid 22%+ taxation on Social Security for decades produces enormous tax savings.

Recent findings suggest that every dollar of AGI pushes you toward the 50% or 85% taxation tiers. Strategic levers include:.

Once you reach age 70.5, you can donate up to $105,000 per year directly from your IRA to a qualified charity. This satisfies your Required Minimum Distribution (RMD) without the distribution being included in your AGI. Lower AGI means lower combined income, which means less Social Security is taxable.

For charitably inclined retirees, QCDs are one of the most tax-efficient giving strategies available — they simultaneously reduce your income tax AND reduce the tax on your Social Security benefits.

Recent findings suggest that delaying Social Security from 62 to 70 increases your benefit by roughly 77%. But there's a secondary benefit: during the delay years, you have more room to do Roth conversions at low tax rates without Social Security benefits adding to your combined income. The combination of larger benefits and lower taxation on those benefits makes delay doubly powerful for tax optimization.

If you retire before claiming Social Security, you have a golden window for Roth conversions. With little or no earned income and no SS benefits, you can convert Traditional IRA money to Roth at the lowest tax brackets of your lifetime. Every dollar you convert is a dollar that will never increase the tax on your Social Security benefits. This window closes permanently once you start claiming.

A step-by-step walkthrough for estimating what you owe.

Industry observers note that list your AGI from all sources: IRA/401(k) withdrawals, pension income, wages, dividends, capital gains, rental income. Get your total Social Security benefit from your SSA-1099 form.

Pro tip: Don't forget nontaxable municipal bond interest — it counts in the combined income formula even though it's not on your 1040.

Add your AGI + nontaxable interest + half of your Social Security benefits. This "combined income" number determines your taxation tier.

Compare your combined income to the thresholds: Single — $25K (50% tier), $34K (85% tier). Married filing jointly — $32K (50% tier), $44K (85% tier).

For the 50% tier: take 50% of combined income above the lower threshold (capped at 50% of benefits). For the 85% tier: the calculation is more complex — use IRS Publication 915 worksheet or tax software.

Industry observers note that pro tip: Tax software handles this automatically. If doing it by hand, IRS Publication 915 has the complete worksheet.

Recent findings suggest that the taxable portion of your Social Security gets added to your other taxable income and taxed at your marginal rate. Check if your state also taxes Social Security.

It has been revealed that for single filers, Social Security becomes partially taxable when combined income exceeds $25,000 (50% tier) and up to 85% taxable above $34,000. For married filing jointly, the thresholds are $32,000 (50% tier) and $44,000 (85% tier). These thresholds have not changed since 1993 and are not indexed for inflation.

Industry observers note that no. Social Security benefits are not earned income. They are classified as unearned income for tax purposes. This distinction matters for things like the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC), IRA contribution eligibility, and the Social Security earnings test (which only applies to earned income like wages and self-employment).

It has been revealed that no — and this is why Roth accounts are so powerful in retirement. Roth IRA withdrawals are not included in the combined income formula used to determine Social Security taxation. Converting Traditional IRA money to Roth before claiming Social Security can dramatically reduce the tax on your benefits for life.

According to recent reports, yes. File Form W-4V with the Social Security Administration to have federal income tax withheld from your benefits. You can choose 7%, 10%, 12%, or 22% withholding. This avoids the surprise of a large tax bill at filing time. State tax withholding varies by state.

Industry observers note that social Security benefits are included in the Modified Adjusted Gross Income (MAGI) calculation that determines Medicare Part B and Part D premium surcharges (IRMAA). High-income retirees can pay significantly more for Medicare — up to 3.4 times the standard premium. Managing MAGI in retirement affects both Social Security taxation and Medicare costs.

In a recent development, there have been numerous proposals to reform Social Security taxation, including indexing the thresholds for inflation, raising the taxable percentage above 85%, or eliminating the tax entirely. As of 2026, no changes have been enacted. The thresholds have remained unchanged since 1993, meaning inflation automatically pushes more retirees into taxable territory each year.

Yes, Social Security benefits can be taxable — up to 85% of your benefits may be added to your taxable income depending on your combined income. The thresholds are low ($25,000 single, $32,000 married) and haven't been adjusted for inflation since 1993, catching more retirees every year. The single most powerful strategy is Roth conversions during early retirement years before claiming Social Security. Every dollar in a Roth account is a dollar that won't push your Social Security into the taxable zone. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Victor Yocco, PhD, is a UX Researcher with a focus on AI and the author of Designing Agentic AI Experiences (CRC Press, 2026), Design for the Mind (Manning, … More about Victor ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

The design community has entered a period of conversational tunnel vision. Because Large Language Models (LLMs) are trained on dialogue, the industry has collectively decided that the chat bubble is the natural home for every AI capability. While the chat interface is a viable and powerful option for many tasks, it is one tool in an expansive toolkit. UX and Product teams must be intentional about the modalities we choose for how owners provide their data and commands, and how the system presents its output.

Sources indicate that to pick the best method, you need to think about what the user wants to do, where they are, and how much cognitive effort they are already expending. This guide offers a clear way to figure out the best approach for any product, using two tools to assist in the process: a Task Audit and an Input/Output Alignment Matrix.

Picture a traveler jogging through a loud airport terminal after a sudden gate change. They are dragging their roller bag and carrying a coffee in the other hand. They need to open their airline app to ask the AI assistant where to go. The tool immediately fails the input modality test. It forces the traveler to stop walking, balance their coffee, and type a long booking reference number into a tiny chat box. When they finally hit send, the system fails the output modality test. Instead of flashing a large, high-contrast gate number, the AI returns a dense paragraph explaining the atmospheric weather patterns causing the delay. The actual gate number sits buried at the very bottom.

While they might make the flight just fine, the user won’t forget the moment of anxiety they felt while using the AI tool — an experience that could have served as a way to reinforce a commitment to UX has instead validated the common conception that companies don’t care about or understand customers using their products. In this scenario, the airline built a smart tool, but the interface failed the user. The input required physical dexterity, which the traveler lacked at the time of need. The output demanded a level of reading focus they could not spare. This article will cover how we can avoid this scenario in our AI-powered tools. In order to be successful, we must evaluate the physical and cognitive load of our owners to match both the input and output modality to their immediate intent.

Let’s first discuss the limitations of a chat-based interface.

The allure of the chatbot is easy to understand from a product development standpoint. It is a blank slate. It suggests that the system can handle anything the user provides. However, a text-heavy interface often causes a high adaptation load. This load increases cognitive demands on owners. Over time, this cognitive burden turns into a psychological tax a person pays when changing natural thought processes to accommodate a machine.

Industry observers note that when an interface relies solely on conversation, it imposes a dual burden: a linguistic challenge for input and a cognitive challenge for output. We’ll examine both separately below.

A blank chat box creates a major problem for users who need to discover what a tool can actually do. In a standard graphical interface, menus and buttons provide clear visual cues that signal every available option. A chat box often leads to choice paralysis because users are forced to guess what the AI is capable of. They have to remember the exact phrasing or technical terms required to get the result they want.

Consider a data analyst who wants to find a specific trend in a spreadsheet. In a traditional tool, they might click a filter or sort button. In a chat interface, they must suddenly become a writer and describe that complex logic in a complete sentence. Another example: a manager trying to reorganize a team schedule. Dragging and dropping blocks on a calendar is intuitive. Describing those same scheduling shifts in a text prompt adds a layer of work that makes the task feel more difficult than it should be.

In a recent development, designing for input means recognizing that composing a prompt is a creative act. It requires a person to translate a vague thought into a specific command. For many professionals, this creates a linguistic barrier. A designer might know exactly how they want an image to look but struggle to describe the lighting or texture in a text prompt. In that case, a slider or a color picker is a much better input method than a text box.

Having addressed the linguistic barrier of constructing input prompts, we must now consider the other half of the conversational burden. This is the cognitive cost the AI imposes when it responds in dense blocks of text.

According to recent reports, when an AI responds in long blocks of text, it transfers the interpretive work to you, the user. Text is a serial medium: your brain has to read one word after the next to extract meaning. That takes time. Sequential reading is necessary in many scenarios. Complex legal analysis or reviewing nuanced medical histories requires reading full paragraphs. Teams create friction when they default to text for data that visual formats communicate faster. Visual methods allow parallel processing. You can view a chart and spot a pattern in under a second.

Imagine asking an AI for a project status revision. Instead of a color-coded dashboard, you receive three paragraphs listing every task completed that week. Now you must read the entire response and mentally summarize it to find the one piece of information you needed. The quick visual check has been replaced by a reading assignment.

In a recent development, the cognitive tax of this work compounds with professional stakes. A doctor asking for a patient’s vital signs needs a clear numerical display, not a narrative describing the readings. A stock trader looking for a price spike needs a line graph immediately, not a written description of price movement over the past hour. In both cases, a text response forces the professional through a slow, error-prone extraction process when speed and accuracy are most notable.

It has been revealed that before selecting a modality, practitioners need a shared vocabulary for what the options actually are. The table below maps common input and output modalities to the contexts where each performs best. This is not a ranking. Each modality has a role; the question is always which role it is playing in a given workflow.

Designing for modality inherently requires a strong focus on accessibility. While visual dashboards provide rapid insight for many people, designers need to provide screen-reader-optimized audio alternatives for users with visual disabilities. Modality choices should multiply pathways to information.

Recent findings suggest that table 1: Input and Output Modality Taxonomy. Use this as a reference during the Task Audit to identify candidate modalities before narrowing to a recommendation.

The following FigureFigure 2 illustrates the cognitive spectrum, mapping how mental effort scales across various interaction methods. This spectrum is a critical tool for designers to visualize the shift from low-effort, ambient interactions to high-effort, focused experiences. By understanding where a specific task sits on this spectrum, teams can identify whether a user needs a “glanceable” output that minimizes mental processing or a high-density format that supports deep, analytical thinking.

With this taxonomy established, the next step is to apply a rigorous method to select the optimal input and output combination. Practitioners must ground this selection process in the user’s real-world environment and context.

Industry observers note that to choose the right interaction method, practitioners should complete a Task Audit before interface design begins. A formal Task Audit is the framework that moves teams from assumptions about user behavior to evidence. This process gathers data about the physical, social, and cognitive context in which the work actually happens, which then drives all input and output modality decisions.

Use these four areas of focus to anchor the audit:.

The audit answers two questions for every feature:.

Here is how to gather the evidence to inform your task audit. Use one or more of these common UX research-related methods:.

This is the most direct way to capture how people work in their natural setting, and it provides the richest data for identifying physical constraints on both input and output. Observation is necessary because owners often perform hidden work: small steps or workarounds they forget to mention in an interview, or environmental details they do not think to describe because they have adapted to them.

The Approach: Go to the user’s actual workspace, whether a field site, warehouse, or office floor. Ask them to perform the task you are studying and observe closely.

What to Look For: This method is most revealing for Input Constraints and Output Constraints.

Industry observers note that interviews surface the mental models and decision points that observation cannot capture. They are most valuable for understanding Cognitive Load.

The Approach: Conduct one-on-one sessions with end-users and the stakeholders who manage the outcome. Use a structured protocol focused on a specific task. Ask for stories about past successes and failures rather than general opinions.

Workshops are essential for defining task boundaries and establishing required fidelity levels. Product managers and stakeholders bring foundational knowledge of system requirements; researchers apply audit criteria.

It has been revealed that the Approach: Use workshops to build a shared Task Inventory. Bring designers, engineers, product managers, and business analysts together to map every step of the process. Product managers and business analysts ensure factual accuracy; the research team applies audit criteria to each step.

Once you gather field evidence through these research channels, map your findings directly against the Modality Taxonomy. Each concrete physical or social constraint you document systematically eliminates mismatched interfaces. This process strips away design guesswork, narrowing your architectural choices down to the specific input and output combinations that survive the reality of the user’s environment.

When you ground input and output modality decisions in field evidence rather than interface convention, the resulting design reduces adaptation load for the user and grounds your modality choices in evidence. When you base decisions on field data, you move past interface convention and build a powerful case for the resources needed to create the right experience for your consumers.

Once the audit is complete, the final step is utilizing the Input/Output Alignment Matrix to formalize the connection between user intent and the optimal modality combination.

With Task Audit findings in hand, you can use an Input/Output Alignment Matrix to map user intent to specific modality combinations. This matrix is organized by what the user is trying to accomplish in a given moment. This distinction versus focusing on what your AI is capable of doing matters. If intent changes across a single workday for the same user, the interface should respond to those shifts.

Choosing the wrong modality for the user’s context can lead to user frustration. Customers might feel mentally drained if a lot of information is delivered through a format that is hard to process, like getting a massive status update only in text. They may also start worrying if an action was actually completed correctly when a precise command is buried within a long chat exchange. Finally, the system can force users into finding clumsy workarounds, making them adapt to the machine’s method instead of working in their natural, most effective way.

Table 2: Input/Output Alignment Matrix. Map user intent to modality combinations using Task Audit evidence. The two added rows (Monitoring/Alert and Guided Task Completion) cover common enterprise and mobile scenarios not captured in simpler frameworks.

When teams coordinate these factors, they can move past the automatic default of adding a chatbot. Visual layouts enable rapid scanning. Structured inputs remove the burden of constructing perfect sentences. Audio outputs serve people whose hands and eyes are otherwise occupied.

A real-world scenario where environmental constraints dictated a shift in design strategy best demonstrates the practical application of this matrix and the broader audit framework.

Industry observers note that field technicians servicing high-voltage electrical grids often face a dangerous misalignment of interface modality. Traditionally, these technicians had to rely on ruggedized tablets to access technical manuals and log status updates. However, the physical constraints of the job — wearing heavy protective gloves and working in bucket trucks at significant heights — made interacting with a standard touch interface nearly impossible while on a job site. Additionally, attempting to read complex, text-heavy diagnostic reports on a screen while maintaining situational awareness created a high cognitive load that increased the risk of safety errors.

According to recent reports, to address this, researchers conducted a Task Audit utilizing three specific methods from this article. First, Contextual Inquiry and Observation revealed that technicians often worked in “hands-busy, eyes-busy” states where any manual input was a significant barrier. Researchers observed technicians wearing mandatory thick protective gloves while in the bucket truck, which made precise screen taps nearly impossible and often triggered the wrong commands.

In a recent development, high-altitude environments also introduced severe screen glare from direct sunlight, washing out the display and making text difficult to read even at full brightness. Furthermore, technicians faced the physical safety risk of trying to manipulate and secure a heavy, ruggedized tablet while balanced in awkward positions, creating a distraction that could lead to dangerous slips or equipment contact. These factors, combined with the need to constantly monitor live wires and the surrounding environment, meant technicians could not safely dedicate their eyes or hands to a standard tablet interface, confirming the severity of the eyes-busy and hands-busy constraints.

Second, Focused Interviews with veteran technicians validated the findings from the field. They confirmed that the operational challenges, including the thick gloves, screen glare, and safety risks, were not unique to one location but were commonly experienced across multiple sites, including high-altitude transmission lines and sprawling power substations. This broad confirmation solidified the need for a non-touch, voice-first solution. The interviews also surfaced a critical cognitive constraint: the need for glance verification of vital signs, such as voltage readings and temperature trends, rather than being forced to read a long narrative description of system health. Technicians stressed that their primary need was immediate, unambiguous verification (is this safe? or where is the fault?), not a lengthy diagnostic report, indicating that a text-heavy response was dangerous to their workflow.

These methods confirmed that the environment required a departure from the traditional chat or form-based AI capability interface.

The resulting solution implemented an adaptive modality handoff designed to mitigate the physical and cognitive barriers researchers identified during the research. While active on a job site, technicians utilize voice input to query the system. This method allows them to remain productive while wearing thick protective gloves that would otherwise prevent precise interaction with a touchscreen.

The AI responds with a short audio summary of immediate diagnostic data. This audio feedback bypasses the challenge of screen glare in high-altitude environments and allows the technician to maintain situational awareness of the high-voltage grid without the safety risk of looking away from dangerous equipment. By providing immediate answers to fault locations through audio, the system meets the technician’s need for glance verification through a hands-free and eyes-free channel.

Once technicians return to a truck and secure safety gear, a system automatically hands off workflows to a 15-inch visual dashboard mounted inside a vehicle. A rugged 10-inch field tablet lacks adequate screen real estate for complex schematics. A larger vehicle display allows for parallel processing of historical trend data and wide electrical grid maps. This case study reflects an actual field audit conducted for a national utility provider. Implementing this adaptive approach reduced diagnostic time by twenty percent and increased daily tool adoption among field crews.

Industry observers note that an AI capability is only as usable as the interface that delivers it. Researchers and designers must resist the pull toward the path of least resistance. Building a chatbot is fast and familiar, something we’ve been doing for decades now. Building an interface that feels like a natural extension of how someone already works is harder, and it is the work that matters.

Start by leaving the screen. The Task Audit requires presence in the places where work actually happens: the field site, the warehouse floor, the operating room. The physical and social realities of those spaces are not edge cases. They are the design brief.

The future of AI interface design is a diverse ecosystem: visual, vocal, haptic, and ambient, calibrated to user intent and environmental context. The chat window is one tool in that ecosystem. It is the right tool for specific jobs, and often the wrong tool for the jobs we reflexively assign to it.

According to recent reports, to get started immediately, run a lightweight version of the Task Audit before your next design sprint. Spend two hours observing the workflow in its actual environment. Conduct three to five interviews with the people who perform the task. Bring a PM or analyst into a 90-minute workshop to build a task inventory and apply the four audit questions. You will not have complete data, but you will have enough to make a defensible modality recommendation backed by evidence rather than convention.

I created a Modality Task Audit Template to help guide teams with moving forward. You can download this worksheet and take it directly to your next field observation. It allows design and product teams to document specific physical barriers before writing a single line of code.

Sources indicate that we focus heavily on training smarter AI models. We owe equal attention to human interfaces. A brilliant underlying model packaged in a lazy text interface fails. When you observe actual work environments and align interaction modalities to them, you remove adaptation friction.

Industry observers note that use this worksheet during field observations. It allows design teams to document specific physical barriers before writing code.

Observe users as they perform a primary task in actual workspaces. Check all applicable conditions.

Industry observers note that vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily. When he is not writing, he’s most probably running front-end & UX … More about Vitaly ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Recent findings suggest that we often hear about shiny new tools that change everything (yet again). But in practice, most people don’t need more tools to deal with in their daily lives. What we actually need are better integrations of useful capabilities that neatly align with our existing and established mental models.

Industry observers note that users don’t get excited about shiny upcoming “smart” workflows, or navigating Terminal commands, or jumping between endless back-and-forth chat interactions. They need seamless integrations of useful features to address problems with high severity, high frequency, and a high level of frustration.

I’ve always been puzzled by the notion of “AI-first” products. They might speed up production, but we need to know really well first what we actually want to build. AI-first often doesn’t account for years of small and significant design decisions that have shaped expectations and mental models over the years.

I love the notion of “Quiet AI”. These are tools that are mostly invisible, sit in the background, and do small tasks on the user’s behalf. They never scream for attention but happily assist in repetitive, frustrating tasks that can easily be automated or assisted with a smart helper.

Excellent examples of Quiet AI include Claude’s integration within Microsoft Excel, PowerPoint, and Word, providing assistance in context without disrupting the user’s workflow.

In a recent development, so no wonder that I absolutely love the idea of folder instructions! There, users can define what a folder is supposed to do, based on the purpose they created it for. It sounds much more complicated than it actually is.

The instructions define what the folder is for, how files should be organized, how sub-folders should behave, and what actions can happen inside. Instead of manually maintaining a folder, you set its intent once and let the system follow it.

It has been revealed that it’s a seamless integration of AI helpers just when and where users want and need it. With permissions and actions locally scoped to that specific folder on the user’s machine, unless the user extends access, permissions, or system rules on their own.

Note: For a deeper dive into this concept, you can jump to Karthikeya GS’s wonderful post “Folder Instructions: Instructions For System-Level AI”.

User’s value doesn’t emerge from users having to juggle between multiple applications, views, and sources every few minutes. That’s when they are slowed down, and that’s when they make mistakes.

It comes from helping users do the work they need to do — by reducing frustrations, slowdowns and mistakes, and taking care of tasks that otherwise would take too much time and too much effort to complete well.

Yet again, seamless integrations — a very underused but incredibly impactful way to deliver value fast, without adding the burden of installing and learning yet another tool.

Breaking: Gen Z apps inform approachable wayfinding for V&A East Storehouse

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (779 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On a mission to draw in museum sceptics, Hackney design studio Fieldwork Facility looked to an unexpected source of inspiration when creating the Dezeen Award-shortlisted wayfinding for London’s V&A East Storehouse.
  • The landmark museum, completed by Diller Scofidio + Renfro last May, has been lauded for opening up the V&A‘s storage vault, including 250,000 historic art, craft and design objects, to the public for the first time.
  • The challenge for Fieldwork Facility was to help visitors navigate and interpret this trove of artefacts – especially a younger, more diverse crowd who might normally feel excluded from museums.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On a mission to draw in museum sceptics, Hackney design studio Fieldwork Facility looked to an unexpected source of inspiration when creating the Dezeen Award-shortlisted wayfinding for London’s V&A East Storehouse.

The landmark museum, completed by Diller Scofidio + Renfro last May, has been lauded for opening up the V&A‘s storage vault, including 250,000 historic art, craft and design objects, to the public for the first time.

The challenge for Fieldwork Facility was to help visitors navigate and interpret this trove of artefacts – especially a younger, more diverse crowd who might normally feel excluded from museums.

To speak to this demographic, studio founder Robin Howie decided to borrow a visual language they’re already intimately familiar with.

“We studied popular Gen-Z apps and services to understand how to make Storehouse feel intuitive as soon as you walk through the door,” Howie told Dezeen.

In a recent development, “Cultural institutions can all too often feel like exclusive environments with many barriers to entry. It’s unfortunately far too easy for so many people to walk into a museum, gallery or national organisation and feel a queasy sense of ‘this isn’t really for me’.”.

As an antidote, Howie and his team decided to treat the wayfinding design like an operating system in itself, looking to the UX of much-used apps like TikTok to inform signage and interaction points across the museum.

From the get-go, visitors are welcomed with an “onboarding text” that introduces them to the Storehouse and how to navigate it.

“It’s a moment that purposefully feels like opening an app for the first time where you are given a quick orientation of the experience held inside,” remarked Howie.

The text combines a range of different media, including printed typography, ticker tape screens and recycled paper tiles.

Topped with recycled plastic letterforms, these tiles provide a first introduction to three key colours used to mark different areas across the building.

Yellow points out viewing galleries, green is for the museum’s viewable restoration labs and pink for the Study Centre, which gives the public unprecedented access to the collection through the V&A’s Order an Object programme – a service traditionally reserved for researchers and academics.

It has been revealed that set into aluminium cases, these recycled paper tiles were used to form adaptable, modular signage across the building. Much like a Scrabble tile, each is emblazoned with a single letter, allowing museum staff to adapt the wayfinding based on what objects are currently on view.

“Storehouse’s signage system looks and feels programmable in an analogue way,” noted Howie.

To suit the use across separate tiles, Fieldwork Facility commissioned a bespoke version of the V&A’s brand typeface Spiller that is monospaced.

This technique, normally used for typesetting computer code, involves shaping each letter so it occupies the same amount of horizontal space.

“The resulting Spiller Mono helps give V&A East its own unique language that is atypical for a museum,” Howie said.

“We also love that monospace typefaces were widely used in early computers and are still standard for writing and editing code – great nod to the ‘building as software’ concept.”.

On some signs, a colourful, enamelled lava-stone disc provides colour coding, echoing the yellow, green and pink first introduced in the onboarding text.

Several other interventions were also designed to encourage interaction, either from visitors or from staff, who engage with the building both as a museum and an active storehouse.

Recent findings suggest that to provide museumgoers with context and explanation about the pieces on show, Fieldwork Facility created interpretation labels that exist as a modular kit of components, allowing them to be fixed to Storehouse’s standardised crates, palettes and forklift-accessible shelving. Digital templates allow staff to amend these labels without relying on the designers.

The design studio even introduced dedicated “expression points” where visitors can share their opinion with the V&A staff or take part in public polls using a voting coin system.

“The operating system approach welcomes everyone to explore, define their own experience, make connections and have agency within a national institution,” Howie noted.

All of the museum’s signage was designed to be adapted and reused to cut out waste, with icons for permanent fixtures – such as toilets, elevators and floor numbers – screen printed or painted directly onto the walls instead of relying on disposable vinyl decals.

Industry observers note that fieldwork Facility’s graphics for V&A Storehouse East have been shortlisted for graphic design of the year at the 2026 Dezeen Awards. It is up against seven other projects, including the visual identity for Dorte Mandrup’s Arctic whale watching facility and ink-free tea packaging for a Song Dynasty-themed restaurant in Guangzhou.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The Virgin and Child Enthroned (1470s) was bought by the London-based private collection Klesch Collection, which declared prepares in May to loan the painting to the Ashmolean for three years.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A painting by Sandro Botticelli at risk of leaving the UK earlier this year has gone on display at the Ashmolean Museum in Oxford where it was first shown in the 1930s.

The Virgin and Child Enthroned (1470s) was bought by the London-based private collection Klesch Collection, which declared prepares in May to loan the painting to the Ashmolean for three years. The painting was previously exhibited at the museum in 1934–35 when it was attributed to Botticelli's workshop.

The UK government placed an export bar on the Botticelli painting, valued at £10.2m, in May 2025. The UK Department for Culture, Media and Sport stated that the painting had a recommended price of £9,960,000 (plus VAT of £272,000, which can be reclaimed by an eligible institution). The work was sold at Sotheby’s London in late 2024 for £9.7m (with fees).

In a recent development, the painting underwent conservation over the summer to remove discoloured varnish and later retouching, revealing well-preserved details of the Virgin and Child and restoring the original cooler tones, indicates an Ashmolean statement. The painting is also unusual for its generous use of gold leaf, “although earlier Italian painters regularly applied gold to the backgrounds of their devotional works, it was less widely used by Botticelli's time”, add the statement.

The Botticelli painting was housed in the Convent of San Giuliano in Florence in the early 19th century, and was later transported to a small chapel attached to a group of farmhouses in a nearby village. It then passed into the family of Giovanni Magherini Graziani, who sold it in November 1903 to the Italian dealer, Elia Volpi. Harriet Sarah Jones Loyd (Lady Wantage) bought the work in May 1904 for £5,000. The Botticelli painting had been kept at Betterton House, near Wantage, Berkshire, since 1944.

Recent findings suggest that founders A. Gary and Dr. Anita Klesch started the Klesch Collection with the acquisition of a set of Four Seasons by Giuseppe Arcimboldo in 2014. The collection of 15th-to-17th-century European art, which also includes works by Caravaggio, Sofonisba Anguissola and Rubens, is regularly loaned to museums and institutions worldwide.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Film and photography by Jim Stephenson.

The restoration of an art deco pavilion and lido near MacDuff, Aberdeenshire, shortlisted for the RIAS Andrew Doolan Best Building in Scotland Award, features in this video by photographer Jim Stephenson.

The film is the latest in a series being published by Dezeen in collaboration with the Royal Incorporation of Architects in Scotland (RIAS) to highlight the annual award’s 2026 shortlist.

In the video, viewers are shown the Tarlair Outdoor Pool Pavilion, revived by London-based Studio Octopi to bring its tea pavilion and pools fully back into use.

The studio aimed to retain the historic character of the 1930s art deco building, while introducing considered upgrades, including a marble-clad exterior.

“We wanted to pay homage to the art deco period, which the building was originally conceived in,” noted Studio Octopi director James Lowe.

“The green came about really in connection with the paint samples that we took off the railings, and it was decided to go with marble that would give resilience to the environment.”.

Established in 2002, the Andrew Doolan Best Building in Scotland Award is an annual award that highlights Scottish projects, with this year’s winner set to be announced on 26 November.

Comprising three reuse projects, RIAS noted this year’s shortlisted projects tap into “important conversations around community, collaboration, retrofit and reuse”. Shortlisted alongside the Tarlair Outdoor Pool Pavilion is the Paisley Central Library by Collective Architecture and the Edinburgh Futures Institute by Bennetts Associates.

Last year’s winner was a public park renewed by studios Stallan-Brand and LDA Design.

The film and photography are courtesy of Jim Stephenson.

#10050. Designing For Distressed Customers: Why Mental Health Apps Shouldn’t Follow Every UI Fashion

📅 2026-07-09 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3561 w)
📖 Baca
