📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Barkas builds the Kuda brand identity on More Life: a stacked wordmark, custom Kuda Modena type, and a deep Lagos purple.
  • The system starts from a sentence, not a logo.
  • Kuda Modena, a custom face drawn by Erkin Karamemet, sets the name at poster scale in heavy geometric capitals for the wordmark and the More Life lockups, with Suisse International alongside for support.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Barkas builds the Kuda brand identity on More Life: a stacked wordmark, custom Kuda Modena type, and a deep Lagos purple.

The system starts from a sentence, not a logo. "If your bank isn't helping you live more, it's holding you back," Barkas writes, and the identity answers with the pulse of Lagos: a stacked KUDA wordmark in thick geometric capitals, deep purple owning every surface it touches, black as its sharper counterweight. Kuda began as "the bank of the free," challenging the friction and fees of traditional Nigerian banking, and the newly introduced work keeps that challenger spirit, aimed at a generation that wants its money to fund a life rather than sit in an account.

The type does the heavy lifting. Kuda Modena, a custom face drawn by Erkin Karamemet, sets the name at poster scale in heavy geometric capitals for the wordmark and the More Life lockups, with Suisse International alongside for support. The specimen shows the full alphabet in lilac on deep purple, with the custom Naira sign sitting among the euro, dollar, pound, and yen, a small detail that roots the whole system in Nigerian money.

According to recent reports, the grid is the app itself. The home screen sorts everything into three plain groups, Essentials, Cardless Payments, and Lifestyle, each icon labeled in the same weight. The wordmark stacks KU over DA like a stamp, and the studio built four versions of the lockup so the mark stays legible from a billboard down to a card chip. Posters hold the same discipline: one line, one color field, the name at the foot.

Purple is the material here. Deep purple fields carry the type, the app, and the card, with lilac doing the bright work and black stepping in wherever the brand needs to sound serious, which is how Kuda Business reads against the personal product. Hand-drawn illustrations soften the geometry: a Lagos street scene in colored pencil, a woman in a pink robe on the SPEND card, loose doodles of everyday moments. Documentary photography from local photographers keeps the people real and unfiltered.

The system stretches across every surface the bank touches. Three phone screens show the balance, the lilac card, and a PIN pad in one calm row. A billboard puts the stacked wordmark over a woman waving from a car window with the line "Less friction. More life." The stocks screen tracks a holding in dollars on the same purple field. Nothing in the system looks like a bank trying to look expensive; everything looks like a bank trying to keep up with Lagos.

See more from Barkas on their site.

#9939. Healthcare organization opens art gallery near Los Angeles

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (784 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theartnewspaper ↗ Open Full Page

Healthcare organization opens art gallery near Los Angeles

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (784 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, altaMed Health Services, a major healthcare provider in Southern California, is opening an art gallery, library and cultural centre to house its art collection in the Los Angeles suburb of Montebello.
  • Industry observers note that altaMed began collecting art in the 1970s, based on a belief that art is an integral part of holistic well-being.
  • “Our collection focuses on Chicano art," Cástulo de la Rocha, the president and chief executive of AltaMed (and founder of the collection), noted in a statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, altaMed Health Services, a major healthcare provider in Southern California, is opening an art gallery, library and cultural centre to house its art collection in the Los Angeles suburb of Montebello. AltaMed’s collection, more than 50 years in the making, includes works by Laura Aguilar, Graciela Iturbide, Gabriel Orozco and others. Its new 30,000-sq.-ft space, The Alta, opens to the public on Sunday (15 November).

Industry observers note that altaMed began collecting art in the 1970s, based on a belief that art is an integral part of holistic well-being. Since then, its collection has grown to some 4,000 pieces, with about 1,400 of them currently placed in its offices and clinics.

“Our collection focuses on Chicano art," Cástulo de la Rocha, the president and chief executive of AltaMed (and founder of the collection), noted in a statement. "Because AltaMed was founded as part of the Chicano Movement in the 1970s, because I was active in the Chicano Movement, and because our patients and employees can connect culturally with the art.”.

Sources indicate that in recent years, AltaMed has been converting a warehouse on the edge of a shopping mall in Montebello to house its collection. The space will have regular hours for visitors to tour its gallery, see works on shelves and sliding racks in open storage, and watch behind-the-scenes processes of digitisation and conservation. There is also studio space for artist residencies on site.

Patssi Valdez and rafa esparza’s Sacred and Profane Beauty (2026) Courtesy AltaMed.

According to recent reports, “The collection is here to serve the communities that AltaMed is focused on in Los Angeles and Orange County, primarily Latino communities,” Pilar Tompkins Rivas, AltaMed’s chief curator and vice president of arts, tells The Art Newspaper. “So we think about art that is relevant and celebratory of those populations.”.

Some recently acquired and commissioned works also address health and community—such as Sonia Romero’s mural The Fence-Pomona (2026), made expressly for the central communal space in a senior-care facility in nearby Pomona. The mural is 6ft high and 10ft wide, depicting a white lattice fence festooned with roses and the San Gabriel Mountains behind it. It ioverlooks a space used for meals, artmaking and gathering for patients.

Sources indicate that altaMed’s collection runs the gamut of media and spans more than 100 years, although most of the work was made after the Second World War. Early pieces include those of Hernando Gonzallo Villa, a commercial artist who famously designed ads and posters for the Santa Fe Railway. More recent works include drawings, prints and paintings by Carlos Almaraz, Judy Baca, Camille Rose Garcia, Gronk, Frank Romero, Eloy Torrez, John Valadez and Linda Vallejo.

The artist Felicia Montes at La Botánica del Barrio (2026) Courtesy AltaMed.

Recent findings suggest that the first exhibition in the gallery is Patssi Valdez: LA LA LA (until 9 April 2027), featuring photo-based and collage works by a pioneer of Los Angeles’s Chicano art movement. For this show, Valdez re-created some of her photography from the 1970s and 80s—portraits of friends that helped define punk and goth glamour.

Recent findings suggest that she notes she had discussed doing something “out of the box” with AltaMed, and several of the framed work have coloured strips of paper flying out from the frame. To highlight some of her portraits, Valdez added Swarovski crystals to the prints, such as in Divine Dede (2026) and Hot Pink (Mario, Charlie & DeDe) (1983/2025). She also co-created work in collaboration with two younger artists, rafa esparza and Gabriela Ruiz.

In a recent development, it has been more than a decade since Valdez had a solo exhibition. “AltaMed has been a collector of my work for quite a while and has been very supportive," she claims. The firm has purchased Valdez’s paintings and photography, and even one of her signature full-size paper dresses. One of these dresses is in a glass case in The Alta’s open-storage area.

Sources indicate that down the hall are the residency studios. The artist Rubén Esparza is working in one of them, where he has been making multimedia pieces featuring his "ongoing exploration of the cultural significance of Latinx, Chicano and Queer diasporas".

Industry observers note that the other studio has been transformed into an educational apothecary by Felicia Montes and her collective Mujeres de Maíz. La Botánica del Barrio (2026) features displays of samplable traditional herbal teas and tinctures, as well as a decorated pushcart. In the hallway, The Wellness Wall lets visitors put up cards with their own home remedies and healing practices. Visitors have suggested some very practical cures—from "talk to friends" and "travelling" to "Vicks" and "a good mezcal".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that recognized as the world’s most lucrative photography competition, the 15th annual HIPA awards celebrated its winners on November 10, 2026, with Family as this year’s theme. The awards were presented at the Museum of the Future, the torus-shaped architectural landmark in Dubai’s financial district in the United Arab Emirates. The 15th season has been a landmark for the Hamdan bin Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum International Photography Award (HIPA). Over 1,000,000 photographs have been submitted, over 500,000 photographers have participated, and 209 countries have been represented cumulatively since the competition started in 2011.

This season featured five categories: Family, Portfolio (Story-Telling), Sports Photography, General (B&W and Color), and Dreams Through AI, which was a newly created category in response to public demand. Judge Tara Todras-Whitehill, an award-winning photojournalist from the US, promptly pointed out that it is better to keep AI-generated work in a separate category rather than have participants enter it in regular categories.

According to recent reports, the other notable judges were Ivan Pedretti, an Italian professional photographer; Kurt Mutchler, a former Senior Science Photo Editor at National Geographic; Germany’s Laci Perenyi, who has captured 21 Olympic Games; Sami Alramyan, a Kuwaiti documentary and humanitarian photographer for 20 years; American Santiago Lyon, Head of Advocacy and Education for the Adobe-led Content Authenticity Initiative; and Tomasz Tomaszewski, an acclaimed Polish photojournalist, with a Ph.D. from the Academy of Fine Arts in Warsaw.

In a recent development, his Highness Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid bin Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum presented the $200,000 Grand Prize to photographer Pinu Rahman. His early-morning drone shot captured a family sleeping in their fire-devastated home, showing resilience and the human spirit.

Ali Bin Thalith, HIPA’s Secretary General, acknowledged the pivotal role of His Highness Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum in advancing the organization’s mission, recognizing his enduring commitment to promoting HIPA and fostering the global art of photography.

Here are the winning photos and videos of the 2026 competition, along with titles and descriptions submitted by the participating photographers.

Banker and amateur photographer Pinu Rehman bagged the Grand Prize for Under the Same Sky submitted to the Family category.

On 25 November 2025, a large fire broke out at around 5:20 p.m. in Korail, one of Dhaka’s most densely populated informal settlements. Spreading rapidly through narrow lanes of tin, bamboo and wooden structures, the blaze destroyed approximately 1,500 homes and left thousands displaced. Photographed the following morning from above, a family of five sleeps side by side within the surviving concrete walls of their burned home. Around them lie twisted corrugated tin, charred debris, and the remains of neighboring shelters. A few salvaged belongings are gathered close. With their home gone, the family rests together in the only space still available to them.

The First Prize in Family went to Hamid Obaid Al Ali for The Promise of Tomorrow.

Captured during a macro dive, this rarely witnessed underwater moment highlights a tiny female sponge crab sheltering, her claws curled protectively around a dense cluster of developing eggs. The amber mass of eggs, each containing a life not yet emerged, rests against the textured surface of the sponge as the crab holds her position in the surrounding darkness. She will remain with her brood until the young are ready to enter the open ocean, where only a few will survive to adulthood. It is a reminder that parental devotion exists throughout the natural world, in places rarely seen.

The Second Prize was received by Nawaf Alosaimi for The Line.

According to recent reports, A large herd of African elephants moves together across an open, darkened plain beneath a pale, cloud-streaked sky. A great matriarch leads from the front, her long tusks prominent and her wrinkled skin rendered in fine detail by the monochrome light. Younger elephants and calves press close among the adults, their trunks and legs forming a dense, overlapping mass of movement. Low hills and distant mountains sit along the horizon and a solitary elephant trails at the far edge of the frame, suggesting the full scale of the group crossing this vast, sweeping landscape.

The Third Prize went to Subhajit Datta for Framed Connection.

According to recent reports, A glass window on a cruise vessel in Ha Long Bay, Vietnam, becomes both mirror and membrane. A father’s reflection fills the frame, camera raised, while inside a mother and child sit together at a dining table, absorbed in a quiet moment. Beyond the glass, limestone karsts rise from the water and other vessels drift in the distance. Reflection, transparency and light combine interior and exterior into a single seamless image, holding three members of a family together within one composed and layered frame.

The First Prize was bagged by Filip Hrebenda for What the Earth Draws in Secret.

Seen from altitude, the landscape abandons all pretense of the familiar. Glacial channels thread across dark sediment in luminous arcs, their turquoise indifferent to the gravity that shaped them. Along a ridge between shadow and a burning yellow ground, bare trees stand in silhouette — neither quite rooted nor quite free, caught at the threshold between dormancy and something that resembles beginning. The photograph does not celebrate renewal so much as observe it in its raw, unfinished state: a world mid-sentence, still composing itself, legible only to those willing to look from far enough away.

Franco Banfi claimed the Second Prize for Give Me a Ride.

According to recent reports, A split-level view reveals an Olive Ridley sea turtle (Lepidochelys olivacea) resting at the surface of the open ocean while a Brown booby (Sula leucogaster) stands perched upon its olive-green shell. This well-documented yet unlikely relationship sees seabirds using surfacing turtles as floating platforms to roost and to feed on fish that gather beneath them. The turtle, protected as a vulnerable species, is the most abundant sea turtle in the Eastern Tropical Pacific. The arrangement offers a degree of mutual benefit: the booby gains a resting spot, while its presence may alert the turtle to approaching hazards.

Ramiro Torrents won Third Prize for Between Ice and Galaxies.

Sources indicate that at Laguna Torre, near El Chaltén in Patagonia, a rare convergence of conditions produced this panoramic night scene. The sky cleared completely, placing the arc of the Milky Way directly above the mountains, while soft moonlight shaped the landscape below. In a region notorious for violent weather, the wind dropped entirely, leaving the icebergs motionless on a still surface. The composition preserves the true scale and immense depth of the wilderness, holding a fleeting moment of absolute stillness in a landscape defined by change.

Taking home the First Prize honor was Jono Allen for Mahina and Mother.

Recent findings suggest that mahina, meaning “moon” in Tongan, is an albino humpback whale calf, a rarity estimated at one in 40,000. Her luminous white body rests close against her mother’s dark, barnacle-marked skin, the contrast between them striking and immediate. The two are at the start of a 4,000-mile migration to Antarctic waters, accompanied by a chosen male guardian. Active shipping lanes, ghost nets, killer whales, and great white sharks mark the route ahead. Mahina’s white coloring, visible from great distances, heightens the dangers. Her mother and guardian remain close, their protective instincts attuned to her exceptional vulnerability.

The Second-Place award went to Barun Sarkar for Beyond the Threads.

Three children peer through a curtain of tangled threads, their faces only partially visible behind the dense weave. Each face is held at a different depth—two side by side and one smaller figure below—their eyes directed outward with quiet intensity. The threads, loose and cascading, partially obscure yet cannot fully conceal the children’s gazes. The strands represent more than fabric: they stand for poverty, limited opportunity, and the barriers inherited across generations. Yet each pair of eyes remains fixed on what lies beyond, carrying hopes that the threads cannot contain.

The Third Prize was awarded to Thomas Vijayan for Black is Powerful.

According to recent reports, out of the quiet depth of night, a melanistic leopard moves forward along a lit track, wild grass bordering the path beside it. The animal emerges from near-total darkness, its pale eyes fixed and unwavering. Reflected light traces the outline of its form, revealing powerful musculature and the faint marks of old scars. The monochrome atmosphere deepens the contrast between the illuminated ground and the surrounding blackness, giving the scene a stillness that speaks to the leopard’s natural authority as one of nature’s most elusive predators.

The winner of the First Prize was Chi Hui Tang for Between Heaven and Earth.

A snow-covered mountain stands beneath a sweeping lenticular cloud formation, its grand form perfectly mirrored in a glass-still surface where mountain, cloud and sky dissolve into one another. A lone black horse gallops across the vast expanse; its small, dark form the only movement within an otherwise tranquil scene. The landscape exists as a dreamlike vision of absolute stillness, freedom and the enduring, elemental forces of nature.

The Second Prize category winner was Fan Ho Tsang for Dreams We Inherit.

It has been revealed that A high-speed train cuts through a tunnel of light, its sleek white form held sharp against streaks of blue and silver that radiate outward in every direction. The composition exaggerates the qualities of motion, light and perspective to carry the feeling of collective purpose—of generations moving forward together, each one building on the hopes and sacrifices of the last. The train becomes more than transport; it stands as a shared journey through time, carrying the weight of family and the inherited dreams they pass on.

The Third Prize was claimed by Bernardo Hernandez for Surfing the Sunset.

Along the beaches of Coveñas, Sucre, Colombia, a female surfer balances naturally atop a small breaking wave at sunset, warm light reflecting off the sea’s surface. The composition places the human figure in harmonious dialogue with the motion of the ocean, where the liquid textures of the water and the precision of the ride meet seamlessly within the warm, fading glow of the South American shoreline.

Yousef Alzanoon clinched the First Prize for Between Hunger and Fire.

In a recent development, “The weight of war in Gaza unfolds in its most unsparing dimensions. Flares illuminate the city skyline at night, while buildings collapse in clouds of smoke and people move through rubble-strewn streets. Thousands gather around aid trucks, carrying sacks of flour across a landscape marked by destruction. Women press forward with empty cooking pots. Aid packages descend by parachute over coastal tent settlements, while families flee on horse-drawn carts carrying their remaining possessions. Mothers hold severely malnourished infants, and children bear the visible effects of acute starvation. The unfolding crisis bears witness to the profound scale of civilian suffering endured throughout the conflict.

The Second Prize was won by Brent Stirton for Rewilding Rhinos.

“African Parks Network has assumed operational control of the world’s largest captive rhino breeding project, formerly owned by breeder John Hume, which houses over 2,000 southern white rhinos and more than 200 black rhinos. Following the operation’s bankruptcy, ownership was transferred to African Parks as a matter of urgency. The organization now faces the enormous challenge of translocating these animals to secure sites across Africa to bolster threatened populations, all while combating a relentless poaching epidemic. The narrative documents the scale and complexity of what may be the largest rewilding of an endangered species in history.

Don Pettit claimed the Third Prize for Milky Way from Orbit.

In a recent development, “These star-field time exposures were captured from the International Space Station using a customized, homemade sidereal star tracker. Rotating once every 90 minutes, the device counteracts the orbital motion of the ISS, allowing distant stars to be recorded as sharp, fixed points, something previously impossible in orbital photography. Across the expanse, Earth’s thin atmosphere glows with auroras in violet, crimson and gold, while city lights streak across the darkened surface below. The dense core of the Milky Way rises beyond the curve of the planet, with the structure of the ISS appearing in silhouette, a reminder of the human presence from which these views were made possible.

The First Place was won by Hongbin Wu for Winter Game.

According to recent reports, “After heavy snowfall covered the mountainous Guoluo region of Qinghai, China, a group of young lamas cleared the basketball court at their temple and began an impromptu game. The concrete court forms a small island amid the surrounding snow, its dark surface contrasting with the vast white landscape. Dressed in scarlet robes, the young monks gather across the court, some playing while others watch from the edges. Their long shadows stretch across the ground beneath the winter sun. The quiet surroundings and lively game create a striking glimpse of youthful energy within the remote setting of monastic life.

The Second Place went to Faisal Hamada for Blazing Lap.

“A McLaren Formula One car speeds across the circuit beneath a blazing sunset, its trajectory stretching the surrounding light into horizontal bands of amber, gold and deep black. The car appears small and sharply defined against the environment, while its papaya livery blends with the warm tones of the sky. Motion blur transforms the circuit and surrounding atmosphere into sweeping lines of color, emphasizing the speed of the passing car. Against the intensity of the sunset, the highly engineered machine becomes a fleeting silhouette, capturing a dramatic moment where precision, movement and light converge.

Third Place went to Kirill Kudryavtsev for Celestial Flare.

“During the men’s snowboard slopestyle qualification at the Milano Cortina 2026 Winter Olympic Games in Livigno, Valtellina (Italy), Germany’s Noah Vicktor releases into the alpine air above Livigno Snow Park. A luminous circular glow surrounds his airborne figure against a deep cobalt sky. The groomed slope cuts a sharp diagonal across the mountainscape, while Vicktor appears suspended at the center of the natural sun flare. The flare creates a striking contrast between the precision of the competition and the expansive mountain landscape, transforming a fleeting sporting moment into an almost celestial scene.

Véronique de Viguerie is a French photojournalist whose work explores the grey zones of a world too often portrayed in black and white. For more than twenty years, she has worked in conflict zones and societies marked by war, repression and political upheaval, from Afghanistan to Yemen, Iraq, Somalia, Nigeria, Syria and Mali. Yet war itself is not her subject. What interests her is what survives within it: desire, humor, beauty, absurdity, tenderness, resistance and the rhythms of ordinary life.

Industry observers note that she does not photograph beauty in spite of war. She photographs beauty, desire, humor and color because they, too, are part of war. To exclude them would be to create another kind of distortion.

In a recent development, this conviction has shaped her longstanding relationship with Afghanistan, which she first visited in 2003 and later lived in for four years. She has returned repeatedly to document Taliban fighters, civilians, women, families, and the profound transformation of Afghan society.

Her work on women has become increasingly central to this vision. De Viguerie is particularly interested in women living within restrictive or violent systems who are too often represented solely through what is done to them. Her photographs instead explore what they do: how they negotiate, resist, love, organize, protect and reinvent themselves, sometimes claiming power in spaces from which they have long been excluded.

Recent findings suggest that dr. Ali Mohamad is a photographer, documentary filmmaker, educator, and entrepreneur whose work is driven by a passion for visual storytelling and the creative industries. He founded TechMission, a digital media and production platform based in Dubai and serving the GC, alongside an education platform dedicated to empowering aspiring and professional photographers and videographers. Drawing on his industry experience, he shares practical knowledge that bridges technical expertise with creative vision, helping photographers and filmmakers refine their skills, develop their visual language, and approach their craft with greater confidence and purpose.

It has been revealed that kazuyoshi Nomachi (b. 1946) is an internationally acclaimed documentary photographer whose work explores the relationship between humanity, nature, and spirituality. Since his first journey to the Sahara in 1972, at age 25, he has devoted his career to documenting the lives, beliefs, and traditions of people inhabiting some of the world’s most challenging environments.

Sources indicate that his journey to the Sahara profoundly changed his direction. Moved by the strength of people living in its harsh environment, he turned to photojournalism and began a lifelong exploration of humanity’s relationship with the natural world.

Inspired by the contrast between the Sahara’s aridity and the life-giving power of water, Nomachi began documenting the Nile in 1980. He traced the White Nile and followed the Blue Nile, capturing the extraordinary landscapes and communities shaped by these great rivers.

According to recent reports, from 1988, Nomachi turned his attention to Asia. His work in western China introduced him to Tibet’s high-altitude communities and the spiritual traditions of Tibetan Buddhism. Between 2004 and 2008, he explored the sacred origins of the Ganges, documenting the landscapes and traditions central to Hinduism.

From 1995 to 2000, Nomachi photographed the holy cities of Mecca and Medina in Saudi Arabia, documenting the Hajj pilgrimage and the profound devotion of Muslims gathering in Mecca. Beginning in 2002, he explored the Andean highlands of Peru and Bolivia, examining the blending of Catholicism and Inca cultural traditions, a project he has continued to pursue.

Among his many honors are the Photographic Society of Japan’s Annual Award, received in 1990 and 1997, and Japan’s Medal of Honor with Purple Ribbon, awarded in 2009.

Paris Photo’s digital sector offers ‘soft photography’ and vital context

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Two weeks after an abbreviated edition of Art Basel Paris, the 29th edition of Paris Photo has taken over the Grand Palais (until 15 November), where digital art is enjoying a moment in the spotlight.
  • According to recent reports, the world of fine art photography is no stranger to controversies involving digital art, and it is heartening to witness the leading photography fair’s commitment to technological excursions within the medium.
  • This year, the digital sector is accompanied by a pedagogical exhibition programme titled Soft Photography, organised by the École Cantonale d'Art de Lausanne in Switzerland and devoted to contextualising the place of AI and CGI within photography.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two weeks after an abbreviated edition of Art Basel Paris, the 29th edition of Paris Photo has taken over the Grand Palais (until 15 November), where digital art is enjoying a moment in the spotlight.

According to recent reports, the world of fine art photography is no stranger to controversies involving digital art, and it is heartening to witness the leading photography fair’s commitment to technological excursions within the medium. Featuring 12 exhibitors this year, the fourth iteration of Paris Photo’s digital sector has been curated by Marco De Mutiis of the Fotomuseum Winterthur, taking over from Nina Roehrs, who had helmed the first three editions.

This year, the digital sector is accompanied by a pedagogical exhibition programme titled Soft Photography, organised by the École Cantonale d'Art de Lausanne in Switzerland and devoted to contextualising the place of AI and CGI within photography. Spanning an interactive exhibition and talks, Soft Photography aims to offer some much-needed dialogue between the medium’s analogue and digital wings.

Paris Photo 2026 at the Grand Palais in Paris © Grégoire Grange.

According to recent reports, the digital sector certainly contains some AI-generated imagery, such as Newly introduced York- based Heft Gallery’s presentation of Alkan Avcıoğlu’s Disreality series, which is an expansion of the surreal landscape aesthetic he first introduced in a collaboration with Edward Burtynsky. But there are also plenty of analogue images throughout the sector, even photograms, enough to make one wonder just how much of a separate section this really is. A similar dynamic played out in the Zero 10 sector of Art Basel’s Swiss fair last June, where the term “digital art” was used so broadly that it begged the question whether a separate area was really warranted.

Recent findings suggest that noteworthy presentations at Paris Photo include the Venezuelan gallery Carmen Araujo Arte, which is showcasing Alejandro Cartagena’s mosaic-cut collages. Created from found photographs, the series is a manual interpretation of how images are made by generative AI by gathering found pixels. The works ask timely questions about authorship while also, in a rather sweet, analog gesture, highlighting just how much our art-making inevitably differs from that of algorithmic processes. The results are genuinely magnetic and intimate.

Palo Gallery’s installation of works from the artist duo Adrea Orejarena and Caleb Stein’s American Glitch series interrogates simulation theory as well as the nature of our screen-filled reality. Oscillating somewhere between the tone of David Lynch’s series Twin Peaks and surveillance footage, the presentation is a highlight, particularly Glitch Typologies (2020-24), the seven-channel sequence of floating images projected on the walls of a 3m-by-3m glass cube, the projectors hanging on a rod at its core, reminiscent of CCTV cameras. At a time of growing cultural cynicism, Orejarena and Stein offer a welcome reminder that the intersection of photography and technology can be whimsical, conspiratorial and surprising.

Yumo Wu, Old Dream No.1, 2026 Courtesy the artist and Licheng Ling Projects.

According to recent reports, yumo Wu’s solo stand with Licheng Ling Projects spans AI and darkroom analogue manipulation, with the images interspersed in such a manner that technique—though it inspires a certain sense of wonder—becomes secondary to the impact of the image. It is perhaps the best example at the fair of a presentation that moves beyond our fixation with what might be real and how it may have been created, with the artist instead asking her audience to quietly behold the images’ abstract textures. Wu is an emerging artist whose skill and willingness to experiment drowns out the noise, and the results are rather wonderful to behold. In addition to the stand marking her first solo presentation in Europe, one of her images is included in Paris Photo’s selection marking the bicentennial of the invention of photography.

Vincent Fournier, Orchis nubigena [Kunminga Gemina], 2026 Courtesy of the artist and Au Cube.

Vincent Fournier’s Flora Incognita, presented by Au Cube, features large-scale portraits of speculative flowers derived from existing flora and manipulated to depict what may happen to them on another planet, exposed to different kinds of radiation or gravity. The photos may at first register as AI-generated images, but were in fact created with CGI using Houdini, a comparatively old-school software. Each image is presented in a wooden frame with a golden plaque on the bottom featuring the name of the plant, evoking the kind of 18th- or 19th-century botanical illustration that particularly benefits from the aesthetics of the Grand Palais, whose architecture harks back to a time of earnest scientific fascination and discovery.

Industry observers note that the Latest York gallery Nguyen-Wahed’s solo stand devoted to the Los Angeles-based photographer Summer Wagner contains unframed, romantic, large-scale photographs featuring grainy, densely-textured and coolly-lit portraits. The presentation, only digital insofar as the images were shot on a digital camera, deals with our relationship with reality as "we’ve collectively succumbed to the tsunami or cultural and technological changes that have thrown image-making into an existential crisis”, according to the artist.

Summer Wagner, Blue Shift, 2024 Courtesy of Nguyen Wahed and the artist.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, facing the digital sector is Ruttkowski 68’s solo stand devoted to François Hallard’s large-scale Polaroid prints of flowers, with the title “Conversations avec Claude” written by the artist in bold letters at the top of the booth. On the second day of previews, Hallard added “(Monet) not IA” to the title, after countless visitors had presumed the works were related to AI. Evidently Anthropic’s AI engine has eclipsed one of the most consequential painters of the 20th century—at least in its claim to the first name Claude.

Given how much of an impact the nascent field of AI-generated photography has had on photography at large, it is unsurprising that we continue to add disclaimers and coin terms to differentiate the medium’s analogue lineage from its technological step-cousins. Several years ago, the dealer Howard Greenberg told me he favours the term “lens-based” to differentiate the two, and this seemed adequate at the time. But since then, plenty of artists (myself included) have incorporated photographic lenses, enlargers and other analogue tools and processes to experiment with and human-wash digital imagery, so “lens-based” may no longer be up to the task of distinguishing between an image taken with a camera and an image generated with a computer. “Synthetic photography” does have a nice ring to it, although the word itself makes one think of things like latex and carcinogenic sunscreen. Perhaps “soft photography” is the best term, for the moment.

Paris Photo’s digital sector and the Soft Photography programming deftly and quietly tackle the discipline’s ongoing existential crisis by demonstrating that digital art predates many of the technologies we are debating today, and its applications in contemporary photography today are legion.

Inside Nikon’s Fresh Exhibit Celebrating the Art and Evolution of the Viewfinder

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Nikon Museum in Tokyo is hosting a special exhibit that celebrates the viewfinder, one of a camera’s most integral and enduring components, from the analog era through today’s mirrorless models.

While the nature of the viewfinder has evolved—moving from an optical system reliant on a mirror in SLR and DSLR cameras to today’s bright, high-resolution OLED panels—photographers throughout Nikon’s illustrious history have relied on viewfinders to compose their shots.

It has been revealed that as Digital Camera Watch explains, Nikon’s new exhibit, Secrets Behind the Viewfinder, focuses on three primary types of viewfinders: rangefinder, SLR, and mirrorless. Visitors can read about each viewfinder type and its related technology in both Japanese and English, explore viewfinder components, and interact with cameras and models.

The Nikon Museum’s special exhibition project leader tells PetaPixel that their favorite part of the exhibit is “the triangular table where visitors can experience three different types of viewfinders firsthand: rangefinder, SLR, and mirrorless.”.

“By picking up each camera and looking through the viewfinder, visitors can directly compare the three systems and gain an intuitive understanding of how they differ.”.

The leader adds that visitors can take home bookmarks—available in both Japanese and English—that celebrate stories from Nikon’s history of viewfinder designs.

“I hope visitors will take them home and enjoy exploring the stories behind Nikon’s viewfinders in more depth.”.

Nikon says the viewfinder has played an “essential role throughout the photographic process, right up to the moment the shutter is released.”.

Industry observers note that “Nikon has therefore always placed great importance on allowing photographers to concentrate fully on their subjects when looking through the viewfinder. I believe we have been able to maintain this approach for so long because it has been valued and supported by our consumers.”.

Nikon points to two key factors that have enabled it to make such beloved viewfinders decade after decade, starting with its optical technology.

“Nikon has developed comprehensive expertise in optics over many years, spanning everything from the production of optical materials to the assembly of optical instruments. We have also applied our optical technologies in a wide range of industrial fields beyond cameras. This broad base of expertise has allowed us to continuously improve our viewfinders by drawing on the right technologies at the right time. For example, optical technologies from the semiconductor field were applied to the development of screens for SLR cameras,” Nikon tells PetaPixel.

The second factor is the company’s commitment to quality.

“We have continuously gathered and analyzed feedback from photographers and reflected it in our products, while applying that level of quality appropriately across a broad range of camera models,” Nikon continues.

Of course, today’s mirrorless viewfinders are fundamentally different from those in SLR cameras. However, they still rely on extremely clear, sharp optical glass. With its modern electronic viewfinders (EVFs), Nikon claims it has dedicated significant time, energy, and resources to creating the clearest, most comfortable viewing experience possible.

In PetaPixel‘s experience, viewfinders like the ultra-sharp unit on the Nikon Z9 and the exceptionally bright one on the Z6 III have been industry standouts.

Sources indicate that but even in the era of the EVF, Nikon claims a lot has changed. Early EVFs had relatively narrow viewing angles, which required specialized optical designs to work around physical space limitations.

However, with the introduction of OLED displays, wider viewing angles have enabled greater flexibility in optical design, resulting in more compact EVF modules.

“At the same time, we have continued to pursue in EVFs the same principle that Nikon has valued since the days of optical viewfinders: a view that allows photographers to concentrate fully on their subjects,” Nikon says. “One example is the Real-Live Viewfinder in the Z 9. Its dual-stream technology processes image data for recording and live-view data independently and simultaneously, enabling an uninterrupted view through the viewfinder even at the moment of capture.”.

“In this way, Nikon has carried forward its long-standing commitment to a clear and comfortable viewing experience, while evolving it into a new kind of shooting experience that only an EVF can provide.”.

Sources indicate that nikon’s Secrets Behind the Viewfinder exhibition is on now at the Nikon Museum, located at the tech giant’s headquarters in Tokyo. It runs through February 27, 2027.

#9928. Tech Report: How to Use Vectorscope in Lightroom

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1536 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Petapixel ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: How to Use Vectorscope in Lightroom

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1536 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The vectorscope has finally arrived in Lightroom, and it is one of the most useful color tools a photographer can add to their editing workflow.
  • It has been revealed that the vectorscope is a tool that visually maps out the hue and saturation of every pixel in a photo, the same way a histogram maps out the exposure.
  • Sources indicate that there is one more thing to keep in mind.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The vectorscope has finally arrived in Lightroom, and it is one of the most useful color tools a photographer can add to their editing workflow. The vectorscope demonstrated up in Adobe Camera Raw a few months ago, and the examples below were shot there. So, in the video, I was still using a third-party solution called Scopes3 for my edits, but now that it has finally arrived in Lightroom as well, it’s time to talk about it.

It has been revealed that the vectorscope is a tool that visually maps out the hue and saturation of every pixel in a photo, the same way a histogram maps out the exposure. The tool looks like a circular chart with dotted lines for the six main colors around the color wheel, along with dots that show you the values in your images. The closer a color’s dot is to the edge of the circle, the more saturated it is in the photo. There is also a seventh line for skin tones, which I’m going to talk about a bit later. In short, the vectorscope is a tool that turns subjective color perception into exact graphics and eliminates the guesswork when color grading your photos.

Sources indicate that there is one more thing to keep in mind. Even though the vectorscope only displays hue and saturation, the way colors appear on it is still influenced by the exposure level of the image. This isn’t because the vectorscope itself reacts to exposure, but because of the HSL color model Lightroom uses to display our photos. In the HSL color model, the colors in the midtones appear much more saturated than colors in the shadows and highlights.

It has been revealed that for example, in an underexposed photo, the vectorscope displays pretty much everything right around the middle of the circle. But if you push the exposure up significantly, it will show much more color because we now have more information in the photo.

On the vectorscope, neutral gray or desaturated colors appear at the center of the circle. So, to set a proper white balance, I aim to make my colors originate from the middle of the vectorscope. This works because when the white balance is off, everything gets skewed to the point where the middle of the scope is no longer centered on the circle. But this is a fine adjustment; we don’t want to make the vectorscope balanced overall. All I want is to make my colors originate from the middle of the circle. The vectorscope displays every color in my image, so having a blue sky, green vegetation, or warm sunset light will naturally create a distribution that spreads unevenly in different directions, and that’s perfectly fine!

Vital note: Don’t confuse white balance with color grading. Both of the photos above have proper white balance. In the first one, we can see that the blues and strong red light in the photo are originating from the middle of the vectorscope. However, in the image on the right, you’ll notice two separate points appearing closer to the center of the circle. This happens because I’ve applied a Color Response Curve as a color grade, which shifts the color of my white point and causes the almost completely blown-out sky to take on a cyan tint. So, make sure to fix the white balance before applying any color grade to your images; otherwise, you will be correcting against the colors you just added to your photos.

Industry observers note that this one is simple, and honestly, it is one of the easiest ways to make sure skin looks right in a final edit. Whenever we have skin in a photo, we can check the vectorscope to make sure the skin color sits along the skin tone line, ensuring we have the right hues and that the people in our images look great.

Industry observers note that the only problem is that, by default in Lightroom, we only see the vectorscope for the entire image. However, we can hover our mouse over the skin of our subjects, and the vectorscope will display a crosshair for the tones underneath. This can be super useful for situations like an autumn portrait, where lots of elements in the photo could be interpreted as skin tones on the vectorscope. Alternatively, we can create a mask over a person’s face so the vectorscope only renders what’s included in that mask.

This way, we can easily target our adjustments to mitigate a green or magenta tint coming from inaccurate lighting, or eliminate the green color cast from portraits where light filtered through foliage above the subject.

The key is to use the vectorscope as a guide for your corrections rather than trying to force every skin tone to the same hue. For this, I suggest creating a mask that isolates only the skin tones in your photo (Select People → Facial Skin + Body Skin). Then, use the White Balance, Tint, and Hue sliders to gently adjust the selected areas until they align more closely with the skin tone line on the vectorscope. This way, you have a much more controlled correction while keeping the color grade intact in the rest of the image.

Recent findings suggest that keep in mind that not every image needs to have its skin tones perfectly aligned with the skin tone line. For example, the photo on the right has a strong color grade applied to it to simulate cross-processing and hue drifting. In this case, it’s perfectly fine for the skin tones to sit slightly off that skin tone line. This is especially true when working with more stylized edits, where the overall color palette and mood of the image take priority over technically accurate skin tones. The vectorscope should be used as a reference, not a strict rule. As long as the skin tones look natural within the context of the image and the overall color grade feels consistent, there’s no need to force them into perfect alignment.

You can also use the vectorscope to fine-tune an existing color grade or make an image fit better within a specific color palette. This is very useful when you’re trying to achieve a consistent look across a series of photos or when you want to match the colors of an image to a specific color palette reference.

For example, if you’re going for an analogous color palette, where you use colors that sit next to each other on the color wheel, you should see most of your color information concentrated within a relatively small section of the vectorscope. Think warm oranges, yellows, and reds for a sunset-inspired look.

Recent findings suggest that we can also use the vectorscope to fine-tune a complementary color palette. Since complementary colors sit opposite each other on the color wheel, we can use the HSL sliders to make sure the two dominant colors in the image sit perfectly across from each other.

The nice thing about using the vectorscope for this is that you don’t have to guess whether your colors are actually following the palette you’re aiming for. You can see their distribution in real time and use the Hue and Saturation sliders, or the color grading wheels, to gently push individual color ranges toward their desired positions. Of course, you don’t need to force every color into perfect alignment. Think of the vectorscope as a visual guide that helps you build more intentional color relationships while keeping the overall image natural and cohesive.

As a bonus, I like to use the vectorscope paired with a Spyder Checkr Video as a reference for how my cameras reproduce colors under specific lighting conditions.

In a recent development, I start by taking a photo with the color checker in frame at the beginning of the shoot, making sure the chart is properly exposed without clipping any of the patches. Then, I bring it into Lightroom, correct the white balance, and now I can easily see how the light in the environment has skewed the color rendition of my camera.

To calibrate the colors, I will now use the HSL panel in Lightroom to make sure the readings on the vectorscope show a hexagon where all the corners are equally spaced (using the Saturation and Luminance sliders) from the middle of the circle and aligned with their specific target colors (using the Hue sliders).

One important thing to keep in mind is that this process is more of a scene-specific color correction than a permanent camera calibration. In other words, the adjustments you make are meant to compensate for the particular lighting conditions in which the photo was taken, rather than permanently changing how your camera reproduces colors. That’s why I recommend doing this as one of the first steps in your editing workflow, before applying any creative color grading or stylized adjustments. You’ll also get the most reliable results when working with daylight or other relatively neutral light sources, rather than heavily colored or RGB lighting, where certain wavelengths might be missing or exaggerated.

  • According to recent reports, the idea is a sentence, not a logo.
  • According to recent reports, type carries the whole system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mother Design rebuilds the MLB brand identity on Modernize Nostalgia: five custom typefaces, the 1968 batter mark, and the shapes of the game.

According to recent reports, the idea is a sentence, not a logo. Mother Design calls it Modernize Nostalgia: take the most iconic pieces of baseball's visual past, refresh them, and put them back to work for a latest generation. The league wanted its brand to match the changes on the field, new rules and a new platform, Baseball Is Something Else. Nothing here is thrown away. The 1968 silhouetted batter logo, drawn by Jerry Dior, stays exactly as it is, and the wordmark beside it is redrawn for the wider system.

According to recent reports, type carries the whole system. Mother Design built five custom faces with five type designers, each one pulled from baseball history. Nick Sherman redrew Franklin Gothic as MLB Franklin. David Jonathan Ross and Bethany Heck derived MLB Clarendon from the 1845 slab serif. OH no Type Co. cut MLB Script from the script styles stitched across team jerseys. Skye Dillon drew MLB Block, the octagonal face found on old ballparks and uniform numerals. Tipotype made MLB Flare from hand-lettering. One poster sets all five in a single sentence.

Industry observers note that the grid comes from the game itself. Mother Design drew a set of shapes from the field: the rounded rectangle of the MLB logo, the pentagon of home plate, the base lines, the circle of the ball, the field seen from above. Color runs in three registers, Core, Extended, and Expressive, built from blues, reds, and creams taken from past and present MLB logos, then charged with club colors. A brand matrix plots every sub-brand by how close it sits to gameplay and what fans expect, so a ticket app stays plain and a social channel gets to play.

The material is the uniform. Play Ball runs in red script across navy jersey fabric, the letters sitting on the weave. The 1969 World Series ticket, red paper dense with prices, rules, and the centenary logo, demonstrates how much of this history was printed, stamped, and torn at the gate. The batter logo keeps its red and blue halves and its white silhouette on deep navy, unchanged since 1968.

The system stretches across the whole league. One grid holds twenty sub-brand lockups, Opening Day, Rickwood Field, the Tokyo Series, Spring Training, the Home Run Derby, the Draft, each built from the same shapes and type. The work rolled out over a two-and-a-half-year partnership, with events like Rickwood Field and MLB Together developed alongside the league's own design team.

See more from Mother Design on their site.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • When a major artist dies, the tributes that come pouring in often gloss over personal shortcomings, whether the failure to complete educational degrees or the abandonment of wives and children.
  • It has been revealed that earlier this week the Getty filled its largest, 450-seat auditorium with fellow artists, curators, friends and family members of the artist, who died last July only four days short of her 100th birthday.
  • Industry observers note that one of the most powerful tributes came from her eldest nephew, Channing Johnson, who described her as a “true” if untraditional matriarch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When a major artist dies, the tributes that come pouring in often gloss over personal shortcomings, whether the failure to complete educational degrees or the abandonment of wives and children. But the memorial to Betye Saar this week at the Getty Center did just the opposite, setting into relief how powerfully she managed to balance—even integrate—acts of mothering and artmaking. (She also managed to earn her bachelor’s degree at the University of California, Los Angeles in 1949, a time when there were few Black students.).

It has been revealed that earlier this week the Getty filled its largest, 450-seat auditorium with fellow artists, curators, friends and family members of the artist, who died last July only four days short of her 100th birthday. The tone was sombre and celebratory, ending with her brother-in-law Bennie Maupin on saxophone and the band Bayou Bump leading a procession, as Saar had wanted.

Industry observers note that one of the most powerful tributes came from her eldest nephew, Channing Johnson, who described her as a “true” if untraditional matriarch. “She was as impactful and skilful as a family matriarch as she was a gifted artist. She gathered us together whether it was in a back yard or public park. She kept our family history in the forefront of our minds and in the public eye—you can literally see our family in her artwork,” he said, referring to assemblages where she incorporated family snapshots or memorabilia.

Johnson also celebrated Saar’s sense of humour and adventure, noting that she learned to belly dance early on and highlighted off her dance moves in June when she was honoured by the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) at its Party in the Garden gala.

His tribute followed one by MoMA director Christophe Cherix, who recalled Saar’s studio in Laurel Canyon being “unlike any other studio I had ever seen…overflowing with treasures, almost archaeological, with objects patiently waiting sometimes years or even decades to be gathered, recognised [and] assembled into works of art”.

Betye Saar, Girl Children, 1964 © Betye Saar, courtesy of the artist and Roberts Projects, Los Angeles.

Sources indicate that saar’s longtime home and studio in Laurel Canyon is where she developed her deeply spiritualist, Black-centred, female-empowered vision through printmaking and assemblage, most famously using a windowpane to organise the esoteric, celestial images that make up the 1969 work Black Girl’s Window. It is also where she raised her three daughters: the sculptor Alison Saar, the mixed media artist Lezley Saar and the writer Tracye Saar. Early on they liked to pretend the wheel of their mother’s printing press was the helm of a pirate ship, and they have said in interviews they are happy they survived without losing a finger or hand.

The veteran Los Angeles collector Joy Simmons, who recalled bringing her week-old daughter Naima to a Saar opening at the Jan Baum gallery in 1981 (“I was not going to miss this opportunity to celebrate a Black woman opening up at a white woman’s gallery”), described the Saar creative lineage, which extends to grandchildren who work in the arts today.

Recent findings suggest that “To Alison, Lezley, Tracye and the whole family: I’ve watched three generations of Saar women make this city’s art history something special. Betye’s work belongs to museums now,” Simmons stated, “but I know her proudest moment and her proudest accomplishment is all of you.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photographer Jasper Cable Alexander has spent the past three years turning up to British dog demonstrates in search of humorous images.

Sources indicate that alexander, who is the son of Royal photographer Lord Snowdon, lost sight in his left eye after a freak accident. He spent ten days in hospital, six months with vision in only one eye, a cornea transplant, and at least eight operations.

Industry observers note that it was a tough time. But he found solace in humor, using it to bring a little lightness and fun to an otherwise difficult situation.

His dog project grew from that instinct. After three years of traipsing around Crufts and specialist Chihuahua competitions to village halls, sports centers, and local shows across the U.K., it eventually became a book: A Proper Dog.

Recent findings suggest that what he found was not really about winning. The prizes are often little more than certificates, ribbons, and recognition. The real reward is the ritual, the friendships and the community.

Photographed almost entirely on analog film, the book feels like stepping into a world stuck somewhere between the 1990s and now.

“I wanted it to feel like this kind of timeless warp that you go into that doesn’t feel like part of this world. A lot of the venues are in community halls or sports halls and places that haven’t really changed much since the 90s, so it feels stuck in that era,” Alexander says.

All proceeds from the book will go to Bristol Eye Hospital, which helped the photographer regain his vision.

Industry observers note that the title of the book, A Proper Dog, asks the question: what makes a proper dog? Many people laugh at Chihuahuas, dismissing them as yappy rodents, but Alexander asks: is all that matters the love between a dog and a person?

According to recent reports, “A Proper Dog is about humour, tenderness and observation. It is a book made to raise money, but mostly to make people smile,” a press release adds.

Industry observers note that the book was released this week, and there will only be 600 to 1,000 copies. The book costs £20. Purchase information can be found here.

Italy Fines Meta $887 Million for Accessing Users’ Photos Stored in Their Phones

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Italy’s Data Protection Authority has fined Meta €805 million ($887 million) for accessing photos and videos stored in Android users’ phone galleries through Facebook without obtaining specific consent or providing adequate information about how the content would be used.
  • The regulator says the feature, known as “Get suggestions from gallery when browsing Facebook,” breached the European ePrivacy directive, which protects smartphones as part of an individual’s private sphere and requires “free and informed consent” before accessing personal content.
  • An investigation found that the feature was enabled by default and that Facebook sought access to users’ photo galleries through a single permission covering several app functions with different purposes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Italy’s Data Protection Authority has fined Meta €805 million ($887 million) for accessing photos and videos stored in Android users’ phone galleries through Facebook without obtaining specific consent or providing adequate information about how the content would be used.

The regulator says the feature, known as “Get suggestions from gallery when browsing Facebook,” breached the European ePrivacy directive, which protects smartphones as part of an individual’s private sphere and requires “free and informed consent” before accessing personal content.

An investigation found that the feature was enabled by default and that Facebook sought access to users’ photo galleries through a single permission covering several app functions with different purposes. The regulator says the information provided to users did not clearly explain that granting access would allow Facebook to generate suggestions for posts using images and videos stored on their devices.

Meta has been given 60 days to disable the feature by default and introduce a separate consent process for its use. The authority notes the decision affects approximately 20 million Android users in Italy.

In a recent development, the penalty was imposed on Meta Platforms Ireland Limited, which disputes Italy’s jurisdiction over the case. The regulator indicates it considered the large number of people affected, the fact that the feature remained active for some customers, and Meta’s “lack of co-operation” during the investigation. The fine represents approximately 0.47% of Meta’s global turnover.

Euronews reports that the investigation began in July 2025 following a complaint from the Bolzano Consumer Protection Centre and was supported by a technical analysis conducted by Italian authorities. The proceedings did not examine whether owners’ content had been used to train AI models, an allegation Meta has denied.

Meta says it will appeal the decision, disputing the regulator’s assessment of the facts, its interpretation of the law, and the size of the penalty.

“We strongly disagree with the [regulator’s] assessment of the facts, its application of the law and the disproportionate level of the fine,” a manufacturer spokesperson tells the BBC.

“This is a straightforward feature which helps people post photos and videos to Facebook. People must give permission on their device before it can operate and they can change this permission at any time via their settings.”.

Last year, PetaPixel reported that Meta was testing an AI-powered feature that processes owners’ photos on their devices.

  • According to recent reports, this week, the newly-renamed ADAA Fair returns to the Park Avenue Armory (until 16 November), the first solely under the leadership of Kinsey Robb, who joined in 2024.
  • Sources indicate that “It’s a continuation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, since 1989, the Art Dealers Association of America (ADAA) had hosted its Art Show, which brought member galleries from across the country together for an annual fair in Fresh York. Last year, the ADAA cancelled the 2025 fair less than four months before it was set to open, citing a need to take a “strategic pause” to reevaluate how to best serve its members.

According to recent reports, this week, the newly-renamed ADAA Fair returns to the Park Avenue Armory (until 16 November), the first solely under the leadership of Kinsey Robb, who joined in 2024. Despite the new name and a few tweaks, it remains the same fair, she notes.

Sources indicate that “It’s a continuation. It's an evolution,” Robb says. “It is still a small-scale collegial fair of the members, so that hasn't changed either. It's just adapting into the environment and the time that we're in.”.

One of those newly introduced aspects is a smaller exhibitor list. This year, 63 galleries are participating, around 12 fewer than the last edition. The intention was to give the fair more focus in a time when dealers and collectors alike are complaining of "fairtigue", both due to frequency and size (Art Basel Miami Beach, the largest art fair in the Western Hemisphere, will also scale down participating galleries this year).

In a recent development, the hiatus “gave us an opportunity to look at the oversaturation of fairs that were happening at that time, and the fatigue that people were feeling,” Kinsey notes. “This scale feels nice to me.”.

The reduction allows for a larger space around the circular bar at the center of this year’s fair, affording attendees more space to move and cut through the three-aisle expo. Visitors naturally found themselves socialising at the centre of the fair during the opening gala for the Whitney Museum of American Art on Thursday (12 November), which was well-attended despite the stormy weather and even a tornado warning in Fresh York City. (During the ADAA fair's hiatus, its longtime preview night partner and beneficiary, the Henry Street Settlement, teamed up with the Independent fair.).

The partnership with the Whitney Museum has brought in a new, often-younger crowd, participating dealers say; works on display, meanwhile, skew heavily toward Modern and post-war secondary-market material rather contemporary works.

“I think deeply about the ecosystem of the art world, and how we all are connected,” Kinsey notes. “Even if we all are in our own lanes or bubbles, we are all essential to each other in service of the art and in service of the artist.”.

The dealers participating range from stalwarts like Hirschl & Adler and Kraushaar Galleries, founding members of the ADAA who participated in the Art Show’s inaugural edition in 1989, to first-time exhibitors like Alexander Berggruen, Sargent's Daughters, Piero Atchugarry, Nicodim and Hollis Taggart.

Sources indicate that taggart has run his namesake gallery for nearly 50 years but only recently became an ADAA member, he says, allowing him to apply for and participate in the fair for the first time. He says that in the first few hours of the opening gala, he saw a great crowd of visitors, often from the surrounding Upper East Side, different from the crowd that comes to the openings in Chelsea, where he has a space. The gallery is presenting a dual stand dedicated to two women Abstract Expressionist painters: Michael (Corinne) West and Teruko Yokoi.

Recent findings suggest that “I think it's very mixed, it’s a bifurcated market,” Taggart indicates of the art market leading up to the fair. “There’s so many daily events that happen politically and financially, like the meltdown with Nvidia. I think the market's OK, but when you consider world events, it's a miracle that it's still as good as it is.”.

The most valuable transactions reported to date at the fair are Agnes Pelton’s The Well of Peace (1932), which had an asking price of $2.4m, and Beauford Delaney’s Untitled (Paris) (1986), which was priced at $1.6m, both from the stand of Upcoming York-based dealer Jonathan Boos.

Another Upper East Side local, Kraushaar Galleries, reported the sale of two paintings for six-figure sums, as well as several works priced below $2,000. James Barron Art says it sold works by Beverly Pepper, Kenneth Noland and Kikuo Saito, each priced between $40,000 and $85,000, while Yoshii Gallery sold several works priced between $6,000 and $80,000. The Chelsea-based gallery and advisory firm AH Arts sold a work on paper by Helen Frankenthaler for $75,000. The international gallery Perrotin sold out of works by Susumu Kamijo, whose paintings on the stand were priced between $30,000 and 45,000. Jessica Silverman from San Francisco reported eight sales from its presentation of fresh works by Julie Buffalohead, ranging in price from $22,000 and $50,000.

According to recent reports, the Tribeca-based dealer Charles Moffett, who previously took part in the 2024 edition, states he appreciated the 2025 break and how the ADAA doesn’t pressure members to take part. During the opening gala, Moffett’s gallery sold four paintings by Lily Stockman priced at $20,000 apiece, and three paintings by Julia Jo priced at $30,000 each.

Recent findings suggest that “With so many of the fairs, once you're on the hamster wheel, it's like, go go go. You apply every year, and if you don't apply or if you decide to sit out a year, you go to the back of the line,” Moffett indicates. “I'm just grateful that this feels more like an organisation that wants to see the best for each gallery.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple’s smart glasses will reportedly begin shipping before the end of 2027 and may have multiple cameras.

Sources indicate that according to a new report by Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, Apple intends to unveil its upcoming smart glasses at WWDC in 2027. The company hopes the device will be its flagship new product of the year.

“After the planned WWDC 2027 unveiling, glasses shipments would begin before the end of the year,” Gurman writes in his latest Power On newsletter for Bloomberg.

In terms of design, Apple’s internal prototypes are slightly thinner than Meta’s second-generation Ray-Ban glasses. Gurman also refers to multiple cameras on the company’s smart glasses, while current eyewear models on the market feature only one.

He claims Apple is testing designs with cameras built into oval-shaped openings that sit flush with the frames, rather than protruding from them. The glasses also feature a front-facing indicator light to show when they are in use or charging. Apple has been experimenting with other features on the front of the glasses related to privacy.

Sources indicate that the first version of the glasses will not include augmented reality (AR), meaning they will not display digital information or images over the user’s view of the real world. Instead, Apple is relying on Siri AI and its extensive App Store ecosystem to help distinguish the product from competing smart glasses. The glasses will integrate with apps that people already use on their iPhones, removing the need for developers to create separate applications for the eyewear.

“Apple is counting on integration with the apps people already use on their iPhones to be a key differentiator for the glasses,” Gurman writes.

Apple is considering several ways Siri AI could work with third-party apps on the glasses. These include making restaurant reservations through an app like OpenTable, booking a ride through Uber or Lyft, ordering coffee through a Starbucks integration, shopping on Amazon, and purchasing movie tickets through an app like Fandango. Third-party applications will not run directly on Apple’s smart glasses, at least in the first version. Instead, they will remain on a paired iPhone, with the two devices working together to handle requests. The approach is similar to Apple’s original smartwatch strategy.

Industry observers note that under current plans, the glasses will require a recent iPhone and will not support Android devices. This arrangement is intended to compensate for the limited computing power and memory available in the eyewear. Apple is also placing an emphasis on industry leading audio quality, with the glasses expected to support phone calls, music playback, and FaceTime audio communication.

According to recent reports, the glasses will also feature Wi-Fi, allowing some functions to continue working when the paired iPhone is not nearby. For example, consumers could continue listening to audio over Wi-Fi after walking away from their phones. However, the glasses will not operate as a fully independent device.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

LIFE Magazine has begun publishing regularly again after a 26-year hiatus, and Olympic figure skater Alysa Liu is on the cover this week, photographed by Spike Jonze.

Jonze is a filmmaker and photographer who made his name in the world of skateboarding before moving into music videos and directing films like Being John Malkovich.

Liu won the gold medal for Team USA at this year’s Winter Olympics in Milan-Cortina. Given Jonze’s skating background, he was a great pick to shoot Liu on the ice and LIFE has released a video detailing exactly how he did it.

Jonze says he set out to capture what it feels like for Liu when she’s out there on the ice. “The first thing I thought would be really cool was to do these really dreamy, streaky photos,” Jonze explains.

Jonze achieved this by using a tungsten lamp (constant light source) and a strobe light synced to his camera.

Using a two-second exposure, Jonze pressed the shutter at the exact moment he wanted to capture. The long exposure meant he could then “streak” the camera, either by panning or zooming, making additional ghostly images of Liu, allowing for creative expression.

“I kind of moved the camera around to almost paint with the color of her dress or her face and it becomes very impressionistic,” Jonze states.

Jonze then made a second setup, which was borrowed straight out of his skateboarding days.

“It was multiple strobes of a trick caught on one frame of film,” he notes. “So again, I would do a two-second shutter, but I would take the flash off-sync from the camera and just manually press the button and go ‘pop, pop, pop, pop, pop’ and pop the strobe as many times in the two seconds as it can recharge in.”.

The resulting image captures an entire trick or sequence from beginning to end on a single frame.

“The first time I did it was with Natas Kaupas or Jeremy Klein, who were pro skaters in the late 80s and so I thought I would try to do a version of that, but more impressionistic,” Jonze explains.

Recent findings suggest that “I wanted it to be all on top of each other so you couldn’t quite see the beginning and the end. It was a blur of the different shapes that she takes when she’s going through the course of the tricks. And that’s what these photos are; they’re sort of the dream images of Alysa’s world of skating.”.

LIFE has published the interview with Liu and Jonze’s photos on its website.

Sources indicate that in 1982, Puerto Rican artist Papo Colo installed a book-shaped sculpture in the courtyard of El Museo del Barrio in Harlem. Commissioned as part of David Hammons’s Art in the Park program, it unfurled like an accordion across a series of 8-by-4-foot plywood panels co-authored by nearly 40 invited Latest York artists and poets. Four decades later, seven of those panels form the basis of Octopus and Others, an exhibition that addresses the porous boundary between the word and the image within the more experimental scenes of production from the ‘80s through today.

The first panel in the exhibition is by Colo himself and gestures toward the alchemical, even transcendent possibilities unleashed through the collaboration of artists and poets across distances, languages, and generations. “English Spanish $ Spanglish,” Colo scribbles in white paint against the black-coated plywood. “Vivas poetas individuales X-formed by Colo’s ceremony into collective.”.
