💡 Key Takeaways
  • Film camera repairer and enthusiast Pierro Pozella has released a website with an ambitious aim: to document every film camera ever made.
  • Pozella of PPP Cameras has spent 15 years repairing, restoring, and selling analog cameras.
  • “I’ve always wanted to find a way to organize that knowledge into something accessible to everyone,” Pozella tells PetaPixel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Film camera repairer and enthusiast Pierro Pozella has released a website with an ambitious aim: to document every film camera ever made.

Pozella of PPP Cameras has spent 15 years repairing, restoring, and selling analog cameras. So there is perhaps no one better placed than him for this project that he calls the Camera Index.

“I’ve always wanted to find a way to organize that knowledge into something accessible to everyone,” Pozella tells PetaPixel.

Recent findings suggest that “There’s a tremendous amount of information out there, but it’s scattered across old books, websites, forums and manuals. Some cameras are incredibly well documented, while others have very little information available.”.

Camera Index features illustrations, technical information, instruction manuals, and external links to sample shots.

Pozella says that it is easy for technical knowledge of something niche like film cameras to disappear — Camera Index is his attempt at centralizing that knowledge into one resource.

Industry observers note that “I also wanted something that was straightforward to navigate. Being autistic, I personally find information much easier to process when it’s clearly organised and presented without unnecessary clutter. That has influenced how I’ve approached the design and structure of the website,” he notes.

“Ultimately, I wanted to create the sort of resource I wish had existed when I first started working with cameras.”.

Industry observers note that pozella has already included 1,300 cameras on the Camera Index, and that’s just for the launch. The website is a long-term project that he intends to work on for a number of years.

“Nobody seems to have a definitive answer to exactly how many analog camera models have been produced,” he says.

“We’re talking about well over a century of camera manufacturing, with thousands of manufacturers producing everything from mass-market consumer cameras to extremely obscure models that were only manufactured in small quantities.

“The number promptly grows when you start considering different variations, regional models and cameras sold under alternative brand names.”.

Pozella has opted for illustrations rather than photos since he doesn’t have access to every single camera model ever made.

“The Camera Index is about making camera information accessible and signposting people to useful information under one roof,” he explains.

“As well as the practical limitations of having to source and photograph over 10,000 plus cameras — I opted for illustrations as they provide a standardized way of identifying each camera. They function as simple visual references or thumbnails for each camera and are not intended to replace photography or be the main focus of the project.”.

Pozella claims the Camera Index is for anyone with an interest in analog photography: from people completely latest to it and looking to buy their first camera, to seasoned collectors looking for information about a particular model.

“More than anything, I hope that the Camera Index will become a lasting reference for analog photography,” he adds.

“A lot of the knowledge surrounding older cameras exists in ageing publications, discontinued websites or in the heads of people who have spent their lives working with them. As time passes, there’s a genuine risk that some of that information will disappear.

“I’d like to help prevent that by bringing together as much information as possible and making it freely accessible.”.

“In the longer term, I also want to expand the archive beyond cameras themselves, documenting accessories and more obscure photographic equipment,” he adds.

“I’m already building a useful links section to connect visitors with camera repairers, specialist shops, manuals and other valuable resources. I think it’s crucial that the archive doesn’t just document cameras, but also helps people find the information and services needed to keep using them.

“If Camera Index eventually becomes somewhere people instinctively go when they want to learn about an analog camera, then I’ll feel I’ve achieved what I set out to do.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the National Gallery of Canada (NGC) and the Sobey Art Foundation named the artist Lotus L. Kang asthe winner of the 2026 Sobey Art Award during a ceremony on Saturday (14 November). The Toronto-born, New York-based photographer, sculptor and installation artist won the 23rd edition of the annual award, the most high-profile and lucrative prize devoted to Canadian contemporary artists, and will receive C$100,000 ($70,000).

The other five shortlisted artists—Melaw Nakehk'o (from the Circumpolar region), Samuel Roy-Bois (Pacific), Audie Murray (Prairies), Caroline Monnet (Québec) and Shane Perley-Dutcher (Atlantic)—will each receive C$25,000 ($17,500), while the 24 longlisted artists each received C$10,000 ($7,000), bringing the total value of the award to C$465,000 ($325,800).

Industry observers note that in a statement, Jonathan Shaughnessy, the chair of the jury for this year’s Sobey Art Award, praised Kang for “the commitment and rigour demonstrated in her practice for well over a decade”. He continued: “Through installations using unfixed photographic film, cast and found objects, and fabricated armatures, her practice resists the stabilising impulses traditionally associated with photography. Reoccurring motifs including lotus root, flowers, soju bottles, birds, anchovies, are not fixed objects, but repositories of place, longing and desire.”.

Partial view of Lotus L. Kang's installation In Cascades (2023-24) in Whitney Biennial 2024: Even Better Than the Real Thing at the Whitney Museum of American Art Photo: The Art Newspaper.

Kang, a recipient of a Guggenheim Fellowship in 2024 whose work was included in the 2024 Whitney Biennial and the 2025 Shanghai Biennale, works across sculpture, photography and site-responsive installation. Her materially dense, non-linear installations explore the liminal space between industrial and architectural forms, familial and social histories, as well as poetry and non-human figures. One of her celebrated installation works, Mother (2020), comprised dozens of metal mixing bowls filled with scattered abstract clay, rubber and stone sculptures as well as aluminium casts of fruit and anchovies. Her critically acclaimed solo exhibition at 52 Walker in Newly introduced York last year featured several greenhouse installations as well as one made of strips of film extended around a spinning rotary dryer.

“It is an honour to be recognised by this prize,” Kang said in a statement. “I am grateful to those I love, those who love me and those who have supported me; you keep me going. The recognition of this prize means that askew ideas are worth pursuing. Art is essential to life, progress and love.”.

In a recent development, during the ceremony, Kang told those assembled at the NGC and those watching via livestream: “I just want to congratulate the other artists. It’s an honour to be nominated alongside you. Shane, Melaw, Caroline, Audie, Samuel. It is really inspiring to be showing alongside you, and who knows what would have happened, and I’m just glad we’ll all keep making art, because it’s really the best thing. So, thank you so much.’’.

It has been revealed that lotus L. Kang, Receiver Transmitter (49 Echoes I), 2022-25 © Lotus Kang. Photo: Courtesy of the artist and 52 Walker gallery, Latest York.

According to recent reports, rob Sobey, the chair of the Sobey Art Foundation, offered his “heartfelt congratulations” to Kang and added: “We also celebrate tonight all 29 artists on this year’s longlist and shortlist for their creativity and vision. We are proud to champion their work and grateful to the National Gallery of Canada for helping bring these remarkable artistic voices to audiences at home and around the world.”.

Selected by an independent jury of curators and cultural leaders, Kang was chosen following a rigorous review process. The jury, who evaluated the artists’ practices, achievements, and contributions to contemporary art in Canada included Kimberly Phillips, the director of the Marianne and Edward Gibson Art Museum at Simon Fraser University, representing the Pacific region;Daisy Desrosiers, a curator at large for North America at Tate, representing the Quebec region;and Helen Nisbet, the director of Glasgow International, serving as international juror.

Works by all six shortlisted artists are presently featured in the 2026 Sobey Art Award Exhibition at the NGC in Ottawa (until 3 January 2027).

According to recent reports, the late Frank H. Sobey, an enthusiastic collector of Canadian art, established the Sobey Art Foundation in 1981 and the Sobey Art Award was debuted in 2002. Five years ago, the award’s criteria were amended from a prize devoted to “emerging artists” under 40 to recognising artists of any age who are at a “critical juncture” in their careers. Past winners have included Brian Jungen (in 2002), Annie Pootoogook (2006), Abbas Akhavan (2015), Laakkuluk Williamson Bathory (2021) and Nico Williams (2024).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Lomography has declared the Lomo72, a new 35mm half-frame analog camera that captures 72 frames per 36-shot roll.

Recent findings suggest that this is actually Lomography’s second half-frame camera of the year, following the Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Half Frame the tech giant unveiled in July. Like that camera, the fresh Lomo72 records a vertical 17x24mm image on half of a standard 35mm frame, fitting two photos onto a single frame. Where a typical 35mm camera captures a horizontal 36x24mm shot, the Lomo72 captures two 17x24mm ones.

As Lomography indicates, photographers can get creative with this. They can capture 72 “normal” shots or create diptych compositions on a single frame, pairing two thematically related shots side by side. Lomography also notes that the vertical orientation of the Lomo72’s photos is “perfect for sharing on social media.”.

It has been revealed that the Lomo72 separates itself further from the Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera through its build quality and design. While both cameras sport a relatively similar squarish look, the Lomo72 opts for a more robust design and a glass lens. Although Lomography hasn’t revealed the complete optical formula, it confirmed that the 27mm lens features a fixed f/8 aperture. Thanks to its half-frame design, the 27mm lens offers a 40.5mm-equivalent field of view. The lens can focus as close as 0.4 meters (1.3 feet).

Recent findings suggest that the Lomo72 has a decidedly old-school design, like many of Lomography’s cameras. It’s quite stylish, though it is presumably made mostly of plastic given its $79 price tag. It has an optical viewfinder and, in good news for all the trendy shooters out there, a traditional flash. The built-in flash also works with colorful gel filters.

It has been revealed that the camera features a 1/100s shutter speed, though it also includes a bulb mode for long exposures. It also has a tripod thread, works with a cable release, and supports multiple exposures.

Analog photography can be quite pricey, so a big advantage of a half-frame camera like the upcoming Lomo72 is that photographers get twice as many shots per roll of film. While users give up a bit of resolution and image area with the format, it is certainly a more economical way to shoot film.

“The Lomo72 Half-frame 35 mm Film Camera is inspired by the golden era of half-frame photography, made for every unhurried, imperfectly perfect moment. It is the kind of camera that makes you smile before you’ve even taken a photo,” Lomography says. “This camera is made for letting the mind wander. It’s about finding creativity everywhere and capturing real moments, ones that you get to relive in nostalgic comfort when you develop the roll.”.

The Lomo72 comes in black and silver colorways, though both feature the same central silver area around the viewfinder and lens. Both versions are just $79.

For customers in Asia-Pacific, the Lomo72 begins shipping this month. For everyone else, including photographers in Europe and North America, shipments start in December. Lomography says that worldwide delivery will occur before December 24, making the Lomo72 a potential Christmas present for analog photographers.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The United States Senate advanced the controversial bill for further debate on November 8 amid mounting criticism from Indigenous groups and historic preservation advocates, largely due to the act's narrowing of Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act of 1966.
  • The law mandates federal agencies to weigh the impact of projects on historic properties, oftentimes with required tribal consultation, though BAAJA removes tribal nations from much of the review process.

Tribal organizations are urging legislators to halt the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), a bill that would speed up the permitting and review processes of major infrastructure projects and could severely undermine tribal sovereignty over sacred and culturally significant sites.

The United States Senate advanced the controversial bill for further debate on November 8 amid mounting criticism from Indigenous groups and historic preservation advocates, largely due to the act's narrowing of Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act of 1966.

The law mandates federal agencies to weigh the impact of projects on historic properties, oftentimes with required tribal consultation, though BAAJA removes tribal nations from much of the review process. The bill text also curtails several other environmental acts, such as the National Environmental Policy Act and the Clean Water Act, and pushes for shorter review timelines, the loosening of protections of sacred lands, and less federal oversight.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

In a recent development, picture this: you're standing at the gate for your Boston weekend trip, and the person next to you just swiped their credit card for $280 to book the exact same seat you're sitting in — a seat that cost you 7,500 Avios and maybe $5.60 in taxes. That's the British Airways Avios short-haul sweet spot in action, and once you see it, you can never unsee it. This is the redemption the ChooseFI community quietly uses to stretch their points further than almost any other domestic award. While everyone else is chasing first-class international awards (which are spectacular, don't get us wrong), this sweet spot lets you turn a modest points balance into a steady stream of nearly free regional flights — year-round, on American Airlines metal, with zero fuel surcharges. Here's the math that makes it click: A last-minute nonstop flight from New York (JFK/LGA) to Boston Logan or Los Angeles (LAX) to San Francisco typically runs anywhere from $150 to $300 in cash. You're paying that for roughly a one-hour flight — the kind of trip where by the time the flight attendant hands you a drink, you're already starting your descent. British Airways prices that same flight at a flat **7,500 Avios**. At a $200 cash fare, that's **2.67 cents per point (CPP)** — well above the standard valuation most programs offer for domestic economy. At a $300 last-minute fare, you're looking at **4 cents per point**, which is exceptional for any award program, let alone a simple domestic booking. The pricing inefficiency is hiding in plain sight: British Airways uses a **distance-based award chart**, which means short flights cost proportionally fewer points. The U.S. domestic short-haul zone (under 650 miles) sits at 7,500 Avios one-way — a price that hasn't ballooned with inflation the way cash fares have. Every time airfare spikes for a holiday weekend or a last-minute booking, your Avios redemption looks better and better. For the FI-minded traveler, this redemption is pure arbitrage: you're converting transferable points that cost you perhaps 1–1.5 cents each to earn into travel worth 2–4 cents each in real-world value. That's a 2–4x return, consistently, on routes you'd likely be flying anyway.

The magic here lives inside British Airways' distance-based award chart — and understanding why it's structured this way is the 'aha moment' that turns a confusing loyalty program into a tool you actually want to use.

Most U.S. airline programs (Delta, United, American) have largely abandoned distance-based pricing in favor of dynamic or zone-based awards that tend to price popular routes higher. British Airways never fully made that switch for partner awards. Their Avios chart still prices flights primarily by the number of miles flown between origin and destination. A flight under 650 miles costs 7,500 Avios one-way in economy — full stop. It doesn't matter if it's a Tuesday in February or the Sunday after Thanksgiving. The chart price holds.

The Partner Piece: Why You're Booking AA, Not BA.

According to recent reports, here's the critical nuance that trips up newly introduced people: British Airways charges notoriously high fuel surcharges on its own operated flights. We're talking $300–800+ in carrier-imposed fees on top of the Avios. That would completely wipe out the value of this redemption. But when you book American Airlines-operated flights through British Airways Avios, those surcharges disappear entirely. AA does not pass fuel surcharges to partner award bookings. Your out-of-pocket cost is typically just the government taxes — often $5–15 each way.

This is the non-negotiable rule: always book AA metal through British Airways Avios, not BA-operated flights.

Avios are one of the most accessible award currencies in the ecosystem. You can transfer from four major transferable points programs at a 1:1 ratio:.

Marriott Bonvoy also transfers to Avios at a 3:1 ratio (3 Marriott points = 1 Avios), and Marriott throws in a 5,000 Avios bonus for every 60,000 Marriott points transferred. That's a less efficient path for this redemption, but worth knowing.

The 355-day booking window means you can transfer and book nearly a full year in advance — critical for holiday travel or high-demand routes.

In a recent development, british Airways allows open-jaw routing on Avios awards. That means you could theoretically fly into one city and out of a nearby city without paying for two separate awards — useful if you're exploring a region and want flexibility. For short domestic hops, this opens up creative itinerary options that pure point-to-point programs don't allow.

Recent findings suggest that before you touch your Avios balance, go to aa.com and run a standard flight search for your route. When the results load, look specifically for flights labeled 'Web Special' or filter by lowest MileSAAver awards. You're searching for American's own award inventory — the same inventory British Airways can see and book. If AA indicates saver-level availability (the lowest award tier), British Airways will almost certainly be able to book it too.

This step saves you frustration. Don't transfer points until you've confirmed the flight you want is bookable at the saver level.

Industry observers note that double-check that your route qualifies for the 7,500 Avios tier by confirming it's under 650 miles. NYC to Boston is about 187 miles. LAX to SFO is about 337 miles. Both qualify easily. A quick Google search — '[City A] to [City B] flight distance miles' — gives you the straight-line distance. When in doubt, routes you'd describe as 'short regional hops' within the same metro corridor will almost always qualify.

You'll pay the Avios from your balance plus the small tax amount with a credit card. You'll receive an American Airlines confirmation number, which you can use at aa.com to manage your reservation, select seats, and add TSA PreCheck or Known Traveler Numbers.

In an open letter published on X (the platform formerly known as Twitter), one of the BFM TV journalists who was attacked states she “truly feared for (their) lives.” According to a report by French news outlet 20 Minutes, the BFM TV journalist says her cameraman was thrown to the ground and beaten, with some protesters shouting threats before stealing his camera. She also says he spent five hours in the emergency room. The extent of his injuries was not specified.

“My cameraman was violently thrown to the ground and then beaten. Some even shouted ‘Burn him!’ before snatching his camera. He spent five hours in the emergency room,” she recounted.

Recent findings suggest that “You can dispute what journalists say. You can criticize their work. You can even hate them. But you don’t hit them,” she added.

Another freelance journalist who witnessed the incident says the cameraman was hit several times and that his camera was smashed and stolen. The journalist also says he had to remove his press badge to avoid being targeted and was struck twice in the foot during the incident.

In a recent development, “It was very, very violent. One of them was hit several times. His camera was thrown to the ground, broken, and then they picked it up and stole it. He was in shock,” the freelance journalist, who publishes under the name Medave Prod on social media, tells Le Monde.

“I had to take off my press badge myself, otherwise I would have been lynched too,” the journalist claims, adding that he had been hit “twice in the foot.”.

An investigation into “intentional violence committed by a group and with faces concealed” was opened, the Lyon prosecutor’s office revealed on Sunday. The investigation also covers “damage to private property,” referring to the journalists’ equipment.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the summer of 1966, David Hockney began work on one of his most iconic paintings: “Beverly Hills Housewife,” a portrait of the arts patron Betty Freeman.
  • According to recent reports, critic and novelist James Cahill uses the painting as a jumping off point to expound on the intertwined lives of both artist and muse, as well as to provide a fragmentary snapshot of Los Angeles in the 1960s, in his latest book.

In the summer of 1966, David Hockney began work on one of his most iconic paintings: “Beverly Hills Housewife,” a portrait of the arts patron Betty Freeman. She is depicted on her garden patio in front of her sleek, modernist house, which is framed by strips of blue sky and green lawn. A few status symbols surround her — a William Turnbull sculpture, a zebra-skin lounge designed by Le Corbusier, and a mounted antelope head— but the focal point is Freeman in her bright pink dress, gazing wistfully beyond the confines of the canvas.

According to recent reports, critic and novelist James Cahill uses the painting as a jumping off point to expound on the intertwined lives of both artist and muse, as well as to provide a fragmentary snapshot of Los Angeles in the 1960s, in his latest book. With The Beverly Hills Housewife: Hockney’s Californian Muse and the World Beyond the Pool (2026), Cahill bounces between formal analysis of the painting, historical anecdotes, and inferences about the broader culture, zigzagging as if driving across LA without a map. Some of the detours prove less relevant to his central narrative than others, but they are nonetheless diverting pit stops on a thoroughly engrossing journey about the friendship between two complex individuals who played formative roles in shaping LA’s cultural landscape.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the UAE is home to a trove of Modernist building designs thanks to the country’s founding in 1971 and the ensuing construction boom.
  • Industry observers note that “Architecture has always been fundamental to Nomad,” states the fair’s founder and director, Nicolas Bellavance‑Lecompte.
  • Simone Crestani’s Forsythia (2026), on show with Lebanese art and design gallery PIK’D at Nomad Abu Dhabi Courtesy PIK’D and NOMAD Abu Dhabi 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the UAE is home to a trove of Modernist building designs thanks to the country’s founding in 1971 and the ensuing construction boom. One such building is the decommissioned Terminal 1 of Zayed International Airport, which was designed by the French architect Paul Andreu and opened in 1982. Now a designated heritage site, it is the unique venue for the Abu Dhabi edition of the itinerant art and design fair Nomad (18-22 November), which returns to the city for a second time in partnership with Abu Dhabi’s Department of Culture and Tourism.

Industry observers note that “Architecture has always been fundamental to Nomad,” states the fair’s founder and director, Nicolas Bellavance‑Lecompte. “[Terminal 1] has a very particular architecture, but also a history as a place of movement and exchange. Rather than placing conventional booths inside it, we wanted to work with the building as we found it—its terminals, corridors, scale and different spatial conditions—and allow those qualities to become part of how the works are experienced.”.

Simone Crestani’s Forsythia (2026), on show with Lebanese art and design gallery PIK’D at Nomad Abu Dhabi Courtesy PIK’D and NOMAD Abu Dhabi 2026.

This year, the fair is expanding that mission with ambitious site-specific takeovers of four of the airport’s private terminals by Nilufar gallery, Gallery Fumi, Galerie Gastou and the jewellery advisory firm A2Z. There are 50 exhibitors taking part this year (compared with 40 last year) including local returning participants such as Leila Heller Gallery and the A/P Room as well as international spaces like Paris-based Galerie BSL, Milan’s Galleria Rossana Orlandi and Carpenters Workshop Gallery from London.

Highlights at the fair will include Maison Intègre’s bronze objects made using the ancient technique of lost wax, cast from recycled metal at its foundry in Burkina Faso; Seoul-based gallery Vein’s pairing of contemporary Korean practices with traditions including ottchil lacquer and mother-of-pearl inlay; and Polish design from Craftica Gallery.

Bellavance‑Lecompte states that jewellery will also be in the spotlight—as well as the 450 sq. m exhibition by A2Z, there will be presentations from the designers Studio Renn, Mattar jewellers and the gallery and advisory Ars Belga/Matthu-Boghossian. The Belgian jewellers Levuma will collaborate with the London gallery JCRD Design to bring together fine jewellery, diamonds and Brazilian design.

Another vital development for Nomad this year is its expanded roster of institutions and non-profit initiatives on show in the old airport’s departure hall. Joining Irthi Contemporary Crafts Council—a Sharjah-based organisation that works with female artisans from the UAE and the wider Middle East, North Africa, South and Southeast Asia regions—which returns for this edition, is the recently established Design Commission Abu Dhabi and a collaborative presentation from the Institut du Monde Arabe (IMA) in Paris and House of Artisans, a cultural centre in Abu Dhabi that preserves traditional Emirati crafts. The project will bring together the French Sudanese fashion designer Abdel El Tayeb, who won the Confirmed Talent category of IMA’s 2024 Design Prize, and Emirati artisans to create a site-specific installation. “[This project] speaks to an idea at the heart of this edition: craft is a living practice, and something new can emerge when makers from different places work together,” Bellavance‑Lecompte indicates.

For Nomad’s inaugural Abu Dhabi edition, galleries reported sales exceeding $20m and many are “returning this year with more ambitious projects”, Bellavance‑Lecompte states. He expects that Abu Dhabi’s expanding cultural calendar and soon-to-open Guggenheim museum will bring more international collectors, curators and attention to the city and to Nomad. “Last year showed us that there is serious interest in collectable design, and this year we can build on those relationships,” he says.

• Nomad Abu Dhabi, Old Abu Dhabi Airport, 18-22 November.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cosina has confirmed the Voigtländer Nokton 35mm f/1.2 Aspherical lens for full-frame Sony and Nikon mirrorless cameras.

Slated to launch next month, the Voigtländer Nokton 35mm f/1.2 Aspherical is a latest and improved version of Cosina’s Voigtländer VM-mount 35mm f/1.2 lens, which the company notes is prized for its “excellent performance and compact design.” The new version has been optimized for mirrorless cameras while maintaining the image quality and silky-smooth bokeh of its VM-mount inspiration.

It has been revealed that as is often the case with Voigtländer lenses, the E-mount and Z-mount versions sport slightly different designs but have the same internal components and optical formula. The E-mount lens has a relatively smooth barrel shape with diamond-knurled focus and aperture control rings. The Z-mount lens, on the other hand, has a scalloped focus ring with vertical ridges and simple ridges on its aperture ring. It also trades red accents for yellow ones, embracing Nikon’s classic color scheme.

It has been revealed that in both cases, the lens is compact. The E-mount lens is just over 60 millimeters (2.37 inches) long and weighs 380 grams (13.4 ounces). The Z-mount lens is 62.4 millimeters (2.46 inches) long and weighs 390 grams (13.8 ounces). Both versions accept 58mm filters.

Recent findings suggest that both manual-focus lenses can focus as close as 0.3 meters (0.98 feet), which results in a maximum magnification ratio of just 1:5.8. Macro lenses these are not. Cosina claims that the manual focusing experience is top-notch thanks to a precise, full-metal helicoid unit and high-quality grease. The tech giant promises “appropriate torque.”.

Optically, the lens features nine elements arranged across seven groups in front of a 12-bladed aperture diaphragm. There are two aspherical elements, and Cosina promises high-resolution performance across the entire frame, even wide open at f/1.2. The firm adds that “color shifts are well controlled,” meaning that the lens minimizes chromatic aberrations.

As for bokeh, a key selling point for an f/1.2 lens like this, Cosina says that out-of-focus areas are “drawn naturally and point light sources, etc., are drawn as soft round bokeh rather than as polygonal shapes.” The aperture ring can also be de-clicked, which should bode well for video applications.

The Cosina Voigtländer Nokton 35mm f/1.2 Aspherical lens will begin shipping next month. While global pricing has not yet been revealed, Asobinet notes that the Japanese price is 140,000 yen, which is around $880. Final global pricing may vary, of course. It is worth noting that the Nokton 35mm f/1.2 Aspherical IV for Leica M-mount is $999 right now thanks to a $150 holiday discount. There’s no word yet on a Canon RF-mount version, although Cosina does make a handful of Voigtländer lenses for Canon mirrorless cameras.

Nearly half of independent publications covering arts and culture in the United States said their business models will not be sustainable without “profound changes” to the current funding landscape, according to a report from Critical Minded and the Dorothea and Leo Rabkin Foundation released this week.

The new survey notably identifies a disturbing correlation between censorship concerns, including external pressure from advertisers and sponsors, and financial precarity. The 41% of respondents who noted they faced free-speech pressures or threats in the last two years were more likely to report funding declines, throwing into stark relief how what outlets choose to cover — or not — may determine whether they can pay staff and contributors, or keep the lights on altogether.

It has been revealed that “Support for Arts and Culture Journalism: A Survey of Independent Publications in the United States” polled 141 independent outlets that cover the arts on challenges impacting the field and strategies used to address them. The anonymized respondents are based in 34 states and the District of Columbia, with the highest concentration (38.2%) in the Northeast, and reach an average annual audience of about half a million.

How to Film and Edit a High Energy Event Sizzle Reel

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1317 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Earlier this fall, I wound up at a music festival in Southern California called Same Same But Different.
  • Industry observers note that I used to regularly film festival sizzle reels and promos over a decade ago, and while I don’t do it much anymore, I still have the muscle memory to capture some good content.
  • First, you have to actually get to the festival.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Earlier this fall, I wound up at a music festival in Southern California called Same Same But Different. I was there helping film a documentary with a friend and decided to actually document my whole process.

Industry observers note that I used to regularly film festival sizzle reels and promos over a decade ago, and while I don’t do it much anymore, I still have the muscle memory to capture some good content. Here’s a crash course on how I used to put together these festival sizzles and recap videos.

First, you have to actually get to the festival. I’ve been to enough of these in the past that I know how to pack light, and thanks to Tucker, The Festival Guy, I had some extra backstage credentials. That remarked, don’t put too much weight on that. Credentials don’t change how you film a festival; they get you a few extra cool angles, but most of what you’ll see here was captured from the GA section, since that’s where the real audience experience lies.

Sources indicate that because you’re capturing something so unpredictable, there are moments happening everywhere, so the first key thing is to always keep a lookout. Scan around you and find people dancing, action moments, anything that captivates and grabs your interest. The second thing I do for these high-energy reels is look for ways to match movement across the camera. If I pan left, I’ll pan left again into the next scene. If I tilt up on one shot, maybe I tilt down out of the next. I’m always editing in my head, picturing how these pieces will fit together.

According to recent reports, the last thing, and maybe the coolest part of festivals like this, is how much color and geometry surround you. I look for ways to build themes out of that. If there’s an umbrella spinning, I’ll find that shape and match it to another sphere or circle somewhere else. Match cuts are a huge part of this, and they add a lot of dynamic energy.

It’s important to note something here about appearance and consent. These festivals often tend to have a very friendly, open, and vibrant crowd, and most people are actually excited to appear in front of the camera and show off their outfits and their moves. Almost all festivals now have a waiver along with your ticket binding the festivalgoer to consent to be filmed, so they can use it for their own sizzle reels. Having mentioned that, you should always approach people with respect, and if you’re unable to ask for consent due to high volume or energy, always visually check in with your subject—if they appear to be uncomfortable, put a hand up, or turn away, then pivot your camera away, give a sign of apology, and don’t use that clip in your edit—always be kind, polite, and respectful.

Recent findings suggest that before I even touch the edit, I always like having music in the back of my mind, a playlist or a selection of some kind, because a piece like this is driven by the track. I pulled up Audiio, our partners, to find it. For this one, I wanted something upbeat. It was an electronic music festival, so I narrowed the genre to electronic, then the mood to energetic. Instrumental only is a good call here so vocals don’t step on the footage or change the tone.

The way I listen is to click through very fast because I know within the first second or two whether the tone, style, rhythm, and pacing will work. I also tend to click into the sections with transitions to find out how the song’s energy moves and develops. There’s a ton to run through, so moving promptly is how I get through it, and I already know the flavor I’m after.

Recent findings suggest that with the song picked, I drop it into the timeline. For the purpose of this sizzle, I trimmed it down to about a minute, landing on that first transition or breakdown before the second part of the song kicks in, which makes for a clean cut. A trick that helps me work faster: I find the different sections of the song and make cuts on the track itself. That helps me remember where each section starts and ends, and snapping to those cuts helps with timing. You can use markers or whatever tools your NLE offers; I like cuts because I can snap to them swiftly.

Recent findings suggest that next are the selects. I run through each shot, set the in and out points, and look for what I was filming for: the transitions and the movements. I’d hold on a shot, whip pan out of it, find another, and whip pan into it, so I want to retain those moments and not trim into them. Then I categorize everything, which keeps me working fast. In this case, I’m using clip color as it’s promptly recognizable. One category is crowd shots: attendees dancing and looking at the camera. Another is transitional elements. Beyond the whip pans and tilts, I was hunting for spherical elements while filming, and I caught a lot of them on the day: parasols, flow toys spinning in circles, staffs people were twirling. Those made great transitions, and it turned filming into a fun challenge, always looking for the next spherical thing to match cut.

Industry observers note that I also separated general B-roll, a walk-through category showing the different sections of the festival and its interactive experiences, a category just for flow toys and tools (poi, fire staff, hoops), stage elements, and stage close-ups. With everything categorized and color-coded, I can drop things in swiftly and track where each element is going.

Industry observers note that I start from my song cuts, and I like to place the transitional elements first—the movements and match cuts with the spherical elements—right on those cuts. Then I use the space in between to fill in as I go. For the opening, I listen to how the song starts slow and ramps up fast, so I want the energy to match that gradual build and sudden explosion into the beat. These will shift around as I work, but they’re bookmarks that tell me which sections are filled. I also had it in mind to move the piece from daytime to nighttime as it progresses.

In a recent development, I like working in these small chunks first, then dialing in the timing so it matches the music. Keeping the music at the forefront as the driving element of these pieces is absolutely key. We cut to the beat, or at least make sure the actions on camera land on the beat. When a fan flies up, I cut on that motion and rise through the next shot with an intentional tilt up into the stage. A rapid zoom or pull-out works too; in one spot, we start on a painting and pull out quickly, right on the rhythm. Another jumps into an abstract shot just as the beat drops, then cuts in on one of those built-in movements—a rapid tilt up matched to the stage lights and lasers.

Industry observers note that with everything in place, the edit is almost done. The last thing I do is go through and add motion transitions where they help enhance the movement I built in. If a zoom or a whip pan isn’t as pronounced as I want, a motion transition can amplify it, really driving a powerful zoom in and out of the next shot. I’ll add just a few, but otherwise the piece is in a good spot.

Recent findings suggest that check out the final video above, and I’ll make sure to post more stuff like this when the opportunity presents itself. Until next time!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A large-scale camera trap survey has revealed that the rarely seen flat-headed cat, traditionally thought to be nocturnal, also roams during the day.

Industry observers note that the flat-headed cat (Prionailurus planiceps), named for its flattened forehead and elongated skull, is one of the world’s rarest and least-studied wild felines. It lives in fragmented habitats across Brunei, Indonesia, and Malaysia. For years, the species has been traditionally considered strictly nocturnal.

According to recent reports, however, a latest study published in Ecology and Evolution has challenged that understanding. Researchers used camera traps to monitor the proposed Lundu Mangrove Protected Forest in southwestern Sarawak, Malaysia, over a nearly three-year period between August 2021 and May 2024.

During the survey, the researchers recorded the flat-headed cat 59 times, revealing an unexpected pattern of activity. According to a report by Mongabay, the camera traps highlighted that the cats were active during both nighttime and daytime hours. Although activity peaked around midnight among flat-headed cats, it also extended into the late morning and afternoon.

The findings revealed “considerable daytime activity,” suggesting that the species’ activity patterns may be more flexible than previously believed. The cameras also recorded an adult female accompanied by a kitten, providing evidence of the species’ presence and possible reproductive activity in the study area.

“This was particularly encouraging because it provides evidence of the species’ presence alongside potential reproductive activity in the study area,” Ahmad Ampeng, the study’s lead author and a research officer at the Forest Department Sarawak, tells Mongabay.

In a recent development, the flat-headed cat is classified as endangered on the IUCN Red List. The species was also once considered possibly extinct in Thailand, until camera traps documented its presence last year, marking its first confirmed appearance there in nearly three decades.

  • The comments were flooded with people disgusted that no one appeared to be taking in the moment, instead watching a real event that was unfolding right in front of them through the small screen of their phone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A video of Christmas lights being switched on in Central London has provoked a debate about people’s picture-taking habits and the importance of living in the moment.

It has been revealed that the video was shared by BBC London on November 4. It highlights a sea of people, seemingly every single one of them with their phones aloft, filming in anticipation of the elaborate lights on Carnaby Street turning on and the fireworks that followed.

A post shared by BBC London (@bbclondon).

The comments were flooded with people disgusted that no one appeared to be taking in the moment, instead watching a real event that was unfolding right in front of them through the small screen of their phone.

Recent findings suggest that “I’ve stopped filming most things like fireworks and concerts when I realized I haven’t watched a single one of them back,” claims Sufian Ahmed. “It’s so much about being in the moment. Experiencing it with the person you’re next to. You lose all that when watching it through a narrow screen.”.

Many compared it to an episode of the Black Mirror TV show, while others called out the people for being “robots.” Others pointed out the hypocrisy of social media people complaining about the video while watching it on their phone.

Previous studies have found that taking a photo of an event affects human memory. A 2018 psychological study suggested that shooting photos or videos gives people a false sense that they preserved a moment, when in actual fact it’s the camera that did it for them.

In 2013, researchers asked one group of people to tour an art museum without taking photos, while another group was assigned to take photos. Those who took photos were significantly worse at identifying items in the museum and recalled fewer details about the items they did remember than those who didn’t take photos.

According to recent reports, dr. Kaitlyn Regehr of University College London and the University of Toronto notes public attitudes toward smartphones and technology are shifting.

“This is not the first year that people have attended events and watched those events through screens,” the smartphone academic tells the BBC.

“But what’s significant is that this year there’s a lot of critical public discourse happening. And that, I think, is really, really positive.

It has been revealed that dr. Regehr says the backlash could be down to “our discomfort with the amount of influence that big tech is playing on our lives.”.

Seven reveals to see in the UAE during Frieze Abu Dhabi

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1565 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Rizq Art Initiative, Abu Dhabi, 6 November-10 January 2027.
  • According to recent reports, in What We Left in the Sandbox, Reem Al Mubarak’s solo exhibition at Rizq Art Initiative, the Emirati artist explores how child’s play can be a powerful medium of creativity and memory.
  • The exhibition is curated by the architect and researcher Azza Aboualam, who was the curator of the UAE’s national pavilion during the 2025 Venice Architecture Biennale.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rizq Art Initiative, Abu Dhabi, 6 November-10 January 2027.

According to recent reports, in What We Left in the Sandbox, Reem Al Mubarak’s solo exhibition at Rizq Art Initiative, the Emirati artist explores how child’s play can be a powerful medium of creativity and memory. Through a series of sculptural works, etchings and drawings, Al Mubarak strives to recall specific places and objects from her own childhood, embracing the distortions of memory. A monumental sandcastle evokes a child’s perspective of space, while bubble wrap that has been compulsively popped or left intact is cast in resin, turning a disposable material into an enduring sculptural form.

The exhibition is curated by the architect and researcher Azza Aboualam, who was the curator of the UAE’s national pavilion during the 2025 Venice Architecture Biennale.

Emirati artist Shaikha Al Mazrou at the Cultural Foundation, where she is staging a solo show Courtesy the Cultural Foundation.

Cultural Foundation, Abu Dhabi, 12 November-15 March 2027.

In 2022, Shaikha Al Mazrou presented her large-scale work Red Stack as part of Frieze Sculpture in London’s Regent’s Park. The work exemplifies her deft approach to defying perceptions through her choice of materials. It features a pile of red cushions constructed from fibreglass and resin on a metal framework. Despite the hardness of the materials, the creased and pillowy cushions evoke a sense of softness.

Sources indicate that she receives her strongest spotlight to date with her solo exhibition at the Abu Dhabi’s Cultural Foundation. It will feature past work alongside new commissions created specifically for the venue’s atrium. Al Mazrou’s work is also on view at Frieze Abu Dhabi with Lawrie Shabibi.

Sources indicate that installation view: All Manner of Experiments: Legacies of the Baghdad Modern Art Group at the NYU Abu Dhabi Art Gallery, 2026. Pictured here: Rand Abdul Jabbar, Earthly Wonders, Celestial Beings (series), (2024).

NYU Abu Dhabi Art Gallery, Abu Dhabi, until 3 January 2027.

Industry observers note that in 1951, Jewad Selim and Shakir Hassan Al Noted established a movement that sought to express Modernist art principles through a uniquely Iraqi perspective. It would prove to be one of the most defining moments of Arab art.

In a recent development, all Manner of Experiments is perhaps the most comprehensive survey of the Baghdad Modern Art Group. It presents seminal works from the period as well as contemporary pieces that highlight the ongoing legacies of the group.

The exhibition at the Newly introduced York University (NYU) Abu Dhabi Art Gallery brings together works from 1946 to 2023, from private and institutional collections. Selim’s experiments with abstraction are represented, as well as Al Remarked’s figurative expressions and his latter work that employed Arabic letters to convey an inner dimension. Key works by Dia al-Azzawi, Madiha Umar and Khalid al-Rahal are also presented, with the exhibition concluding with contemporary pieces by Mahmoud Obaidi, Walid Siti and Rand Abdul Jabbar, among others.

A key point of departure in this show is Selim’s Freedom Monument, a 50m-long sculpture in Tahrir Square that was commissioned just after the 1958 military coup that overthrew the Hashemite monarchy and established the Iraqi Republic. Though Selim died in 1961 before the sculpture fully materialised, it is considered to be one of his most enduring works, potent with the sensibilities that inspired the Baghdad Modern Art Group. Read from right to left—like an Arabic text—the monument tells the story of the revolution. Its bronze figures draw from Sumerian motifs while also employing Modernist aesthetics.

A carved ivory jewelled casket on show in the exhibition Spices and Wonders at Louvre Abu Dhabi © Department of Culture and Tourism – Abu Dhabi; Photo: Sylvie Van Roey.

Louvre Abu Dhabi, until 14 February 2027.

Industry observers note that the Indian Ocean has been a pivotal node of cultural exchange for centuries, and an exhibition at the Louvre Abu Dhabi unravels the ancient maritime connections that linked Europe, Africa and the Middle East to South and Southeast Asia. Held in collaboration with the Guimet Museum in Paris, the exhibition charts these links through artefacts, textiles, ceramics and spices.

Sources indicate that this investigation extends to Art Here—a staple show in Louvre Abu Dhabi’s calendar, presenting works shortlisted for the annual Richard Mille Art Prize. This year’s exhibition, exploring the theme of “Confluences” is curated by Kamini Sawhney (until 28 February 2027).

Recent findings suggest that serendipitously, the theme of Frieze Masters Abu Dhabi also looks towards the Indian Ocean, presenting artefacts, maps and rare books. Presentations at Frieze will contribute to research into an understudied historical topic with implications for the modern era.

Luisa Dörr, various works from Escaramuzas, (2024–ongoing).

Photography Gallery, Sharjah, until 29 November.

The 13th edition of Vantage Point takes place at the Photography Gallery in Sharjah, a venue that opened in November 2025. The exhibition, an annual fixture in Sharjah’s arts programme since 2013, is being held in an overhauled format. Each year, dozens of international artists have taken part in the exhibition, which celebrates photographic works across genres, from photojournalism to more experimental compositions. Vantage Point has now been pared down, exhibiting commissioned works by six photographers, and it will also be a biennial event moving forward.

Sathish Kumar presents a series of images that focus on his brother, an oil worker in Abu Dhabi. Photographs of Kumar’s family in the industrial city compound in Al Ruwais are juxtaposed with those taken in Bengaluru in southern India. Much of the latter centre around the construction site of the family home. The series, titled Bond, alludes to the fraught experiences of many South Asian labourers who travel to the Gulf with the aim of financially supporting their parents and families back home.

The other works featured in the exhibition are equally evocative and personal. Latifa AlBokhari presents tender images that mark key moments in a woman’s life in the Gulf, from henna traditions to wedding preparations. Guanyu Xu reveals life-sized images of domestic interiors that offer clues to the personalities of the people that inhabit them. Luisa Dörr documents with painterly sensibilities a female-focused equestrian school in Mexico. Maheder Haileselassie spotlights archival images of Arbegnoch fighters, who resisted the Italian occupation of Ethiopia between 1936 and 1941. Finally, Adam Rouhana presents larger-than-life portraits of Palestinians from the West Bank, whom he photographed in a travelling studio.

Courtesy of the artist and ATHR Gallery.

The Jameel Arts Centre has given five artists each a dedicated space within the institution.

One room charts four decades of Walid Siti's practice. Sketches of dark, spiralling towers embody the human pathology of scaling literal and proverbial heights. Sculptures and acrylic paintings of mountains, meanwhile, beckon to the peaks of his native Iraqi Kurdistan. A commissioned large-scale sculpture is the centrepiece of the exhibition. It outlines a mountain in stacked polystyrene, with writing on its underside that reflects on the turbulent history of Kurdistan.

Sources indicate that bahraini painter Lulua Alyahya presents the urban and natural environments of the Gulf with diffused brushstrokes. Her work often teeters on the absurd, with lions scowling from computer screens and chickens hatching eggs that fry on the pavement.

Afrah Shafiq is showing Nobody Knows For Certain, an interactive video game work that drawns on a lesser-known but rich period of cultural exchange between India and the Soviet Union that took place between the 1950s and 80s.

Industry observers note that upcoming Dream Machine Project, a three-metre-high installation by Shezad Dawood, is a gyrating tower pulsing with light. Inspired by Brion Gysin’s Dreamachine, which the artist devised after his time in Tangier and after “experimenting with altered states of being” with members of the Beat Generation. The installation was prototyped by artisans in Fes, Morocco, with the final version engineered in Slough, England.

Trembling Hands (2024) by Bani Abidi gathers the artist's portraits of artists, journalists and politicians who spoke out against the genocide of Palestinians, some of whom faced backlash, censorship or repression as a result.

Installation view of Rohini Devasher, Latent Fields (Field Five) (2023); Latent Fields (Field Six) (2023).

Ishara Art Foundation, Dubai, until 15 December.

The sky held it, the earth remembered presents the work of Pakistani artist Shahana Rajani, Indian artist Rohini Devasher and Bangladeshi artist Sarker Protick, all of whom consider how memory and history are preserved and transmitted.

In Rajani’s three-channel video Lines that World a River, a woman paints a house along the banks of a river. The scene is vibrant with its textured blues and chalky greens. Rajani zooms in on the woman’s fingers. Her nails are streaked with the white of the paint she uses to draw the river’s foam. The drawing is of the woman’s ancestral village along the Indus River Delta—now submerged after the construction of hydraulic dams and barrages.

The work—a newly introduced iteration of Rajani’s Four Acts of Recovery, which won the Han Nefkens Foundation’s inaugural South Asian Video Art Production Grant in 2023—indicates how displaced communities in the Indus region have developed mural painting practices to remember their lost homes.

According to recent reports, devasher’s Latent Fields comprises three sprawling silk panels that hang from the ceiling. Their dots and patterns allude to sunspots and other solar events, coming together as a monumental record of celestial time.

In Dhaka 1217, meanwhile, Protick presents 135 photographs that capture the transformation of the neighbourhood where the artist was born and continues to live.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that framed by their car’s windshield, and then again by my rearview mirror, a man and a woman who seem to be a couple look like they'd rather be anywhere but together. He’s behind the wheel, doing all the talking; she’s looking straight ahead, motionless like a marble statue. Gradually, her face wears a desperate expression that only grows more hopeless as he continues talking and gesticulating.

Recent findings suggest that in the supermarket checkout line, I pick up a copy of TIME magazine for the first time in God knows how long, drawn to a painting of Jesus Christ on the cover. It’s a special edition promising to tell us “Who he was. Who he is. His miracles, his mission, his love.” I expect to see a lot of biblical sheep inside, but I don’t find any. I buy the issue as an artifact. I stopped believing in TIME magazine a long time ago.

It has been revealed that down the street, a place that pretended to be a legitimate art gallery for a couple of months, showing the worst possible commercial art, has finally given up, and now it’s selling fur coats. A man in a cowboy hat walks past two girls dancing for a social media video. The air is chilly, and I think of buying myself a leather jacket.

She looks at me with the most loving eyes as she holds a stack of perfectly folded laundry. She comforts me with her wide, auspicious smile, her jet-black hair, and her wrinkle-free, porcelain skin. I feel safe, accepted, and not judged. “Fast service, same day,” she promises because she’s just a model in an ad for a laundromat.

—Hakim Bishara, editor-in-chief.

In a recent development, “As an adult and as a journalist, I have stared shamelessly.” That refusal to look away is precisely what data journalist, writer, and artist Mona Chalabi has built her deeply principled career on. Known best for her indelible data visualizations, from the obscenity of Jeff Bezos’s wealth to the Israeli government’s starvation of Palestinians in Gaza and the racial and gender biases in museum collections, the Pulitzer Prize-winning Iraqi-British journalist tackles the subject of wealth and economic inequality in America in her first book, Ten Lives: How What We Have Shapes Who We Are (2026). | Lakshmi Rivera Amin.

Recent findings suggest that picture this: you're settled into your seat on a United flight out of LAX, the Pacific stretching endlessly outside your window, and you know — you genuinely know — that the person next to you paid $400 for this exact seat while you paid **7,500 miles**. That's the Hawaiian sweet spot, and it's one of the most quietly powerful redemptions available to anyone building a travel rewards strategy. Hawaii has always been the aspirational American vacation. It's the honeymoon destination, the bucket-list family trip, the anniversary getaway. And because of that demand, flights from the mainland — especially during spring break, summer, and the holidays — rarely go on sale. A round-trip economy ticket from Los Angeles to Honolulu will routinely run **$400–$700**, and during peak travel windows, prices can push past $1,000 for a family of four. That's real money. FI-community money. Now consider what Turkish Airlines Miles & Smiles charges for that same seat: **7,500 miles one-way**. At the low end of cash pricing ($200 for a one-way), you're extracting **2.7 cents per point**. At the high end ($500 during peak season), that same 7,500 miles is worth **6.7 cents per point** — a figure that makes even seasoned travel rewards enthusiasts do a double-take. For context, most people in the points world consider 1.5–2 cents per point a solid redemption. **Getting 6.7 cents per point is extraordinary.** It's not a fluke or a loophole — it's a structural pricing inefficiency baked into the Turkish award chart, which treats all short-haul domestic U.S. flights (including Hawaii, which is technically a domestic route) at the same rock-bottom rate. This is the fundamental insight behind every great travel rewards redemption: **loyalty programs price awards based on their own logic, not cash fares.** Turkish Miles & Smiles sees LAX→HNL as a short Star Alliance partner flight. The fact that cash fares on that route are elevated because of destination demand is irrelevant to their award chart. That gap — between what Turkish charges in miles and what the market charges in dollars — is exactly where you save.   • This year’s competition received 27,108 entries from photographers in nearly 100 countries, a record-breaking number for the longtime photo contest.
  • Finnish photographer Hannu Ahonen bested stiff competition to earn the title of Nature Photographer of the Year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Nature Photographer of the Year 2026 winners have been unveiled, showcasing the world’s best nature, wildlife, and landscape photography.

This year’s competition received 27,108 entries from photographers in nearly 100 countries, a record-breaking number for the longtime photo contest.

Finnish photographer Hannu Ahonen bested stiff competition to earn the title of Nature Photographer of the Year. Ahonen’s award-winning photo, “The One that Left and the One that Stayed,” is an extraordinary image of a water lily leaf positioned alongside its icy duplicate.

“It is not often that a photograph of a plant is crowned the overall winner of a major photography competition, but the jury could not overlook this fascinating image by Hannu Ahonen,” notes jury chair Theo Bosboom. “First and foremost, the photograph captures a unique situation: a water lily leaf with an almost perfect black-and-white replica of it lying next to it in the water.”.

Ahonen’s winning photo tells a compelling and unusual story. The living water lily leaf is positioned on the left, while the ice that formed on top of it and slipped off sits delicately to the side, blown away slightly by the breeze. Even the veins from the leaf are visible in the icy shell.

Nature Photographer of the Year adds that the photo reveals the “marvelous beauty of nature” while embodying its transient character. The sheet of ice will soon melt away, joining the water that keeps the lily alive in the first place. It’s a symbolic photo at a time when climate change is impacting all life on Earth, especially its ice.

Sources indicate that “The winter ice had arrived, but it remained snowless for a long time. Some of the pond’s lily pad leaves began to crumble on top of the ice. The wind carried a few of them away, revealing delicate, frosty ornaments left behind. I eagerly captured this natural phenomenon, something I had never witnessed before,” Ahonen explains.

Ahonen has an inspiring story. He has ADHD and lives in a wilderness home in Finland with no carbon footprint. Rarely venturing more than a couple of miles from his home, he spends much of his time behind the camera in his yard, using photography as a spiritual escape and creative outlet.

Alongside the overall winner, Ahonen, the competition’s jury also selected winners across nearly a dozen categories. There are also special prizes for youth photographers and an accomplished portfolio. Ahonen took the top spot in the Plants and Fungi category, so that category is not included below.

French photographer Lucas Mugnier-Lavorel won this year’s Birds category for his environmental portrait of a Magellanic woodpecker in Patagonia.

Recent findings suggest that “Environmental portraits of wildlife can make us feel closer to the animals despite being farther away from them, when done right. This image of a Magellanic woodpecker in its gorgeous habitat was a perfect example. It stood out from thousands of submissions because of its understated sense of place, beauty, simplicity, and timing,” says judge Steffen Foerster.

“Overall, it was a very successful reminder of how the portrayal of nature in its literal state can still be the most powerful of photographic expressions,” Foerster concludes.

British photographer Paul Goldstein’s foggy photo of a giraffe earned the top prize in the Mammals category.

In a recent development, “Quiet images can be easy to overlook in the fiercely competitive mammal category, one of the largest in NPOTY. This ethereal image of a giraffe peeking out of the mist revealed its strengths gradually. Initially a little disorienting, it offered just enough of a visual puzzle to keep the viewer engaged until the image resolved,” Foerster explains.

Recent findings suggest that judges tapped Marcus Kuan’s macro photo of a surprisingly rich and diverse little ecosystem alongside a pitcher plant in the Other Animals category. The Singaporean photographer impressed the panel with his composition and lighting.

In a recent development, “The lighting, colors, and unexpected gathering of species immediately caught our attention. Kuan beautifully captured a world where crustaceans, amphibians, and carnivorous plants cross paths,” explains jury member Louis Guillot.

“As judges, we were drawn to the possibilities unfolding within this single frame. Could the pitchers be digesting invertebrates? Might the frog be exploring a potential egg-laying site, while the crab continues its daily search for food among the plants?” Guillot continues.

Photographer J Fritz Rumpf from the United States won this year’s Landscape category with a silhouetted photo of Iguazú Falls in Argentina.

In a recent development, “What immediately caught our attention was the incredible light and atmosphere in this photo. The longer we looked, the more fascinating it became. There is so much to discover: the last light of day illuminating the mist rising from Iguazú Falls, the silhouettes of trees and rocks, the birds circling above, the sunlight streaming through an opening in the rock at the center, and the subtle waterfall on the left,” says jury member Ilse Koks.

Another American photographer, Matt Pérez, won the Underwater category with a striking photo of a turtle beneath a collection of newt eggs.

“Pérez’s photograph immediately drew us in. As a jury, we wanted to linger over it, exploring the details and wondering what we were seeing,” remarks Guillot. “Newt egg masses decorate the submerged branches like baubles on a Christmas tree, framing the scene and guiding our eyes towards the pond turtle with its piercing yellow eyes.”.

Guillot adds that the scene looks “otherworldly,” which is a very apt description.

Chinese photographer Xuzhong Liu’s abstract drone shot of a winding landscape ticks all the right boxes. It has interesting patterns, striking colors, and a very pleasing composition.

Liu captured the image in a wetland area in China and states the scene strongly reminded him of peach blossoms he had previously photographed—hence the title, “Peach Blossoms in the Snow.”.

Sources indicate that “This photograph has everything that can make a drone shot interesting and fascinating. First and foremost, there are beautiful shapes and subtle colours, but there is also a sense of alienation. What am I actually looking at, and what is the scale of the landscape in the photograph?” asks the chair of the judging panel, Theo Bosboom.

Czech photographer Petr Bambousek’s winning photo depicts a sobering scene of a Malayan sun bear resting inside a garbage incinerator.

In a recent development, “The winning image stood out for its striking depiction of the impact human activity has on local wildlife,” explains jury member Lana Tannir. “The sleeping Malayan sun bear inside a garbage incinerator creates a powerful visual contrast, showing how habitat loss and human waste increasingly force wild animals into close contact with human environments.”.

Tannir says Bambousek’s photo is “unexpected and unsettling.”.

Hungarian photographer László Tóth won the Black and White category for his striking, high-contrast, abstract photo.

Industry observers note that “This photo really stood out to us. At first, we were not quite sure what we were looking at. It sparked some wonderful discussions among the jury and made us look even closer,” claims Ilse Koks.

As for what the photo actually depicts, it’s a thin layer of snow on top of a frozen lake, shaped by the wind.

According to recent reports, this photo might be familiar to PetaPixel readers. Norwegian photographer Audun Rikardsen recently won an award for a similar underwater portrait of a polar bear peering down through a hole in the ice.

It has been revealed that “Just when we thought we had seen about every kind of polar bear image there is, along comes this shot taken from inside a hole in the ice looking up at the bear,” says Steffen Foerster. “Once you realize what is happening, you start thinking about how this shot could possibly have been taken. Then it dawns on you that it seems almost impossible, no matter how.”.

Recent findings suggest that this special category, “De Lage Landen” (which translates to “The Low Countries”), celebrates photos captured in the low-lying region of northwestern Europe, including the Netherlands, where Nature Photographer of the Year is based. This year’s winning photo is by Hungarian photographer Enikő Kálovics.

“The winning image stood out for its ability to transform a familiar landscape into something dreamlike and unexpected,” says Lana Tannir. “The combination of the tiny lacewings, the autumn forest, and the purplish night sky creates a delicate, atmospheric interpretation of the nature of ‘De Lage Landen.'”.

American photographer Parham Pourahmad, who was also recently celebrated in the 2027 North American Nature Photography Association (NANPA) Showcase, won this year’s Youth category with a lovely monochromatic photo of a coyote beneath a large tree.

According to recent reports, “In ‘Tree of Life’, Pourahmad captured a striking scene that could comfortably hold its own in the adult categories,” says Guillot. “Black and white was an excellent choice, defining the coyote’s silhouette and revealing the majestic oak’s intricate network of branches. Even within this wider scene, the coyote’s downward gaze is clear. Pourahmad explained that it was searching for rodent prey, a small detail that brings the photograph to life.”.

Pourahmad has also been named Youth Photographer of the Year.

It has been revealed that the Fred Hazelhoff Award celebrates a portfolio of nature photos, rather than a single image. This year’s portfolio winner is German photographer Simone Baumeister.

In a recent development, “In the portfolio category, the bar is set considerably higher for participating photographers than in the individual categories. Whilst a single fantastic photograph is sufficient there, in the portfolio category you need a whole series of outstanding images that not only complement one another but also fit together well in terms of style and theme. Simone Baumeister has succeeded brilliantly in this with her portfolio on eagle owls in the city,” says jury chair Theo Bosboom.

Baumeister has been fascinated by owls for as long as she has been interested in nature photography. The eagle owl’s story is a positive one, in contrast to the plight of many species across the globe. The species, once on the brink of extinction in Germany, has made an incredible recovery. Its resurgence is thanks largely to major conservation efforts and extensive reintroduction programs.

“It was perched in twilight on a church, right below the street lamps, moving cars, and a string of people passing by, with music blaring from a pub right on the church square. Not a soul took notice of the impressive bird with a wingspan of 1.7 meters flying up the steeple, sitting enthroned right within everybody’s view,” the photographer claims of the first time she saw an eagle owl in a city.

Ever since then, she has been consistently excited by eagle owls and keen to photograph them in many different places. Observing and photographing them in various cities inevitably morphed into a dedicated project.

Alongside the category and special award winners above, the judges also selected runners-up and highly commended photos, all of which can be seen on the Nature Photographer of the Year website and below.

Entries for the Nature Photographer of the Year 2027 open on November 20, 2026.

It has been revealed that image creditsNature Photographer of the Year. Individual photographers are credited in the image captions.

With substantial scholarships, exceptional facilities, accomplished faculty, and private studios, students pursuing an MFA in Studio Art and Design at the University of Louisville have the resources and creative freedom to develop their artistic practice within a dynamic, supportive community.

Recent findings suggest that the rigorous 60-credit MFA program encourages experimentation, critical inquiry, and interdisciplinary exploration. Students may pursue interdisciplinary practices or concentrate on individual media, including ceramics, drawing, glass, painting, photography, printmaking, sculpture, design, upcoming media, and installation.

According to recent reports, located in Louisville's Portland arts district, the MFA program occupies a dedicated, newly renovated warehouse featuring individual graduate studios, state-of-the-art production facilities, laboratories, a seminar room, and an exhibition gallery. This distinctive environment provides students with the space, resources, and opportunities to develop ambitious creative projects.

The Hite Institute also offers a 31-credit-hour MA in Art History or Curatorial Studies. Combining critical theory, art historical research, contemporary art, and hands-on exhibition experience, the program prepares students for careers in museums, galleries, curatorial practice, arts administration, and art writing, as well as further academic study.

Founded in 1946, the endowed Hite Institute of Art + Design has built a distinctive identity grounded in its avant-garde origins and oriented to creative experimentation and critical inquiry. Its accomplished faculty of practicing artists, designers, and scholars encourages students to expand their creative and intellectual horizons while engaging with contemporary cultural, social, and environmental complications.

According to recent reports, both graduate programs maintain small, selective cohorts, allowing for close faculty mentorship, individualized attention, and meaningful collaboration. Students benefit from the Hite Institute's extensive resources, including six galleries, outstanding glass and additive manufacturing facilities, partnerships with museums and cultural institutions, an active alumni network, and visiting lectures by internationally recognized artists, curators, and arts professionals.

In addition to guaranteed scholarships, graduate students may qualify for teaching assistantships, internships, and additional awards that provide valuable professional experience and support their creative and scholarly development.

Applications for Fall 2027 admission are due January 15, 2027.

To learn more, visit art.louisville.edu.

Frieze Artist Award reimagines endangered Lebanese site

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (420 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Theartnewspaper

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • One of Lebanon’s most intriguing archaeological sites is the inspiration behind the inaugural Frieze Abu Dhabi Artist Award, given to the fast-rising Lebanese artist Dala Nasser to create her installation Qubbat Duris.
  • Placed in the atrium of the fair, the work will comprise a timber frame evoking Qubbat Duris’s structure, with fabrics covered in charcoal rubbings of the remaining ruins and painted with ash, raw clay and terracotta draped over it.
  • Nasser is best known for her archaeological frottage paintings—made using the surfaces of endangered historical sites—which consider the artist’s role in reproducing, and bearing witness to, history and landscape.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of Lebanon’s most intriguing archaeological sites is the inspiration behind the inaugural Frieze Abu Dhabi Artist Award, given to the fast-rising Lebanese artist Dala Nasser to create her installation Qubbat Duris. The work takes its name from a 13th-century Muslim shrine near Baalbek, northeast of Beirut, which is composed from the ruins of two separate ancient Roman sites: granite columns from Baalbek’s Temple of Jupiter hold up limestone sarcophagi from a necropolis.

Placed in the atrium of the fair, the work will comprise a timber frame evoking Qubbat Duris’s structure, with fabrics covered in charcoal rubbings of the remaining ruins and painted with ash, raw clay and terracotta draped over it.

Nasser is best known for her archaeological frottage paintings—made using the surfaces of endangered historical sites—which consider the artist’s role in reproducing, and bearing witness to, history and landscape.

According to recent reports, though Nasser is not the first artist to engage with Qubbat Duris, she points out, many of her antecedents are problematic. “The site has already been extensively imagined and reimagined in art historical painting,” she tells The Art Newspaper. “From Orientalist depictions to the backdrop to one of Gertrude Bell’s most circulated photographs, taken in costume on horseback.”.

According to recent reports, similar works of Nasser’s—such as Adonis River (2023) and Wedding at Qana (2024)—have also taken as their subjects “landscapes that loom large in historical painting but look nothing like the landscape itself in Western Asia, either overwhelmed by Orientalist tropes or painted as scenes of European countryside, betraying the artists’ lack of knowledge and limits of imagination”, she says. “I am trying to make paintings that are truthful to the landscape.”.

According to recent reports, the question of “truth” pertains to Qubbat Duris’s position as a site that reflects the layered cultural histories and religions of Lebanon. “It exists as a palimpsest from the second century AD until today, carrying all of the traces in between,” Nasser says.

Meanwhile, the role of evidence and recording in Nasser’s practice also considers the risks of erasure faced by much of Lebanon’s cultural artefacts, particularly from Israel’s longstanding and continued occupation of the country. On 15 October 2024, Qubbat Duris sustained slight damage from Israeli airstrikes; previously during the 2006 Israel-Lebanon war, an Israeli airstrike dislodged one of the shrine’s stones. “I’m interested in how a place like Qubbat Duris carries physical evidence of everything it’s endured, including scars of damage,” Nasser says.

• Frieze Abu Dhabi, Manarat Al Saadiyat, 19-22 November.
